info.title: DYNO Mapper Public API
info.description:
## Introduction

The DYNO Mapper API works on the same projects the application does. A project is the sitemap of one
site: crawl it, import it or build it by hand, then edit its tree, read its inventory, comment on its
items, test its pages for accessibility and track where its keywords rank.

Paths below are relative to `https://api.dynomapper.com` and begin with `/v1`. Every response is
JSON. Requests carry a bearer token, and [Authentication](#authentication) covers how to get one.
Each operation has its own page in the reference; this page covers what they share.

## Concepts

Every operation uses these words the same way. Each is explained here once, rather than on the page
of every call that needs it.

| Term | Meaning |
| :--- | :------ |
| account | What the API is scoped to. Projects, keywords and reports belong to an account rather than to a user, so every member of the account sees the same data. |
| project | The sitemap of one site, with its inventory, comments and accessibility runs. A project is created by a crawl, by an import or by hand, and counts against the plan's project allowance. |
| sitemap item | One row of a project's tree. An item of type `link` stands for a page of the site; one of type `container` groups other items and has no URL of its own. |
| bucket | Not a separate object: `buckets` on a project is the number of published `container` items, which is why it never overlaps `pages`. |
| content block | One stored piece of an item's body, such as a `richtext` or `text` block, each with its own `id`, `properties` and `settings`. |
| crawl | The queued job that walks a site from a start URL and writes what it finds as sitemap items. It reports `PENDING`, `RUNNING`, `PERSIST` and `FINISHED`. |
| accessibility run | One check of a project's pages against a guideline set such as `WCAG22-AAA`. The `id` of a run is the `reportId` every other accessibility endpoint takes. |
| keyword and market | A search phrase tracked for one project in one locale on one device. A market is the country and language that a `locale` code stands for. |
| assignment | A task recorded against a project and, optionally, one of its pages: the users it is assigned to, its state (`open` or `completed`) and a free-form `metadata` object. |
| VACQ | A project's score out of 100: the mean of the visibility, accessibility and content-quality pillars. |
| DACQ | The same score with discoverability in place of visibility, used for a private SharePoint project where ranking data says nothing. |
| file key | The handle that `POST /v1/files` returns for an uploaded file. Passing it to an import saves sending the file again. |

The settings a crawl takes are described field by field on `POST /v1/project/url`, which is the only
operation that accepts them.

## Authentication

Two ways in, ending in the same place: a bearer token in the `Authorization` header. A **Personal
Access Token** is the shorter path for a script or a personal tool. **OAuth 2.0** is for software
that acts for somebody else, and the token it receives is bounded by that user's account.

### Personal access token

1. Generate a token on the [Personal Access Tokens](https://app.dynomapper.com/developer) page —
   the same page that creates an OAuth application and gives you its `Client ID` and `Client
   Secret`.
2. Send it as a bearer token:

```http
Authorization: Bearer ACCESS_TOKEN
```

`ACCESS_TOKEN` is the token copied from that page. Treat it as a password: it carries the access of
the user who created it, and the API neither shows it again nor recovers it.

### OAuth 2.0 authorization code flow

1. Authorize the user, with PKCE.
2. Exchange the code for an access token.
3. Refresh the token when it expires.
4. Send it as a bearer token.

### 1. Authorize

Redirect the user's browser to `GET /oauth/authorize`.

| Parameter               | Type   | Description                                                                                       |
| :---------------------- | :----- | :------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| `response_type`         | string | Must be set to `code`.                                                                            |
| `client_id`             | string | Your application's Client ID.                                                                     |
| `redirect_uri`          | string | The URL where the user is redirected after authorization.                                        |
| `state`                 | string | An opaque value used to maintain state between the request and callback.                          |
| `code_challenge`        | string | The S256 digest of your code verifier, base64url and unpadded. See [PKCE](#pkce-rfc-7636).        |
| `code_challenge_method` | string | Must be `S256` when `code_challenge` is sent. Omitting it is refused rather than assumed.         |
| `scope`                 | string | Not implemented. Accepted and ignored: a token's access is bounded by the account that grants it. |

#### PKCE (RFC 7636)

PKCE ties the authorization code to the client that asked for it, so a code intercepted on the
redirect is useless without the verifier that never left your process. This server supports **S256
only**, and says so in `GET /.well-known/oauth-authorization-server` as
`code_challenge_methods_supported: ["S256"]`.

1. Generate a **code verifier**: 43 to 128 characters from `A-Z a-z 0-9 - . _ ~`, using a
   cryptographically secure random source.
2. Keep it, and send the **base64url encoding of its SHA-256 digest**, without padding, as
   `code_challenge` — 43 characters.
3. Send `code_challenge_method=S256` with it. Leaving the method out is refused rather than assumed:
   RFC 7636 defines an omitted method as `plain`, which this server does not accept, and silently
   treating it as S256 would fail your exchange later for no visible reason.
4. Send the verifier as `code_verifier` when you exchange the code in the next step.

```bash
CODE_VERIFIER=$(openssl rand -base64 48 | tr -d '=+/' | cut -c1-64)
CODE_CHALLENGE=$(printf %s "$CODE_VERIFIER" \
  | openssl dgst -binary -sha256 | openssl base64 -A | tr '+/' '-_' | tr -d '=')
```

A client with no secret — every client created by dynamic registration — **must** use PKCE. One
that has a secret may skip it; a code issued without a challenge carries none and is exchanged as
before, so turning PKCE on here broke nothing that already worked.

Getting it wrong answers `400` on the exchange, and the `error` tells you which mistake it was: a
missing `code_verifier` for a code that was issued with a challenge is `invalid_request`, and one
that does not match the challenge is `invalid_grant`.

### 2. Obtain an access token

After the user authorizes your application, they are redirected back to your `redirect_uri` with a
`code`. Exchange it with `POST /oauth/token`.

| Parameter       | Type   | Description                                                                            |
| :-------------- | :----- | :------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `grant_type`    | string | Must be set to `authorization_code`.                                                   |
| `code`          | string | The authorization code received from the redirect.                                     |
| `redirect_uri`  | string | Must match the `redirect_uri` used in the authorize request.                           |
| `client_id`     | string | Your application's Client ID.                                                          |
| `client_secret` | string | Your application's Client Secret. Omit it if your client is registered without one.    |
| `code_verifier` | string | Required when the code was issued with a `code_challenge`. See [PKCE](#pkce-rfc-7636). |

```json
{
  "access_token": "...",
  "refresh_token": "...",
  "expires_in": 3600,
  "token_type": "Bearer"
}
```

### 3. Refresh an access token

Access tokens are short-lived. Exchange the `refresh_token` for a new one with `POST /oauth/token`
when the current one expires.

| Parameter       | Type   | Description                                                |
| :-------------- | :----- | :--------------------------------------------------------- |
| `grant_type`    | string | Must be set to `refresh_token`.                            |
| `refresh_token` | string | The refresh token obtained from the initial token request. |
| `client_id`     | string | Your application's Client ID.                              |
| `client_secret` | string | Your application's Client Secret.                          |

### 4. Send the token

Both flows end here:

```http
Authorization: Bearer ACCESS_TOKEN
```

## First request

`GET /v1/user/me` needs no id and reads no project, so it is the cheapest check that a token works:
the call to make first when a request fails and you want to know whether the credential or the
request is at fault.

```bash
curl https://api.dynomapper.com/v1/user/me \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer ACCESS_TOKEN"
```

```json
{
  "id": 12,
  "accountId": 34,
  "email": "someone@example.com",
  "name": "Someone",
  "company": "Example Ltd",
  "thirdPartyProviders": []
}
```

`ACCESS_TOKEN` is the token from the Personal Access Tokens page, or the `access_token` the token
endpoint returned. `accountId` is the scope everything else works in, which is why it is worth
reading before your first project call.

## Workflows

Most endpoints here stand alone. The tasks below do not: each is a sequence, and the calls only
make sense in order. Find your task, follow its steps.

| Task                            | The calls                                                                                       |
| :------------------------------ | :---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Crawl a website                 | `POST /v1/project/url` → poll `GET /v1/project/url/{id}` → `GET /v1/project/{projectId}`        |
| Crawl a private SharePoint site | `POST /v1/project/sharepoint` → poll `GET /v1/project/url/{id}` → `GET /v1/project/{projectId}` |
| Import a text or XML file       | `POST /v1/project/text` → poll `GET /v1/project/text/{id}` → `GET /v1/project/{projectId}`      |
| Create an empty project         | `POST /v1/project/scratch` → edit its items → `GET /v1/project/{projectId}`                     |
| Upload a file, then import it   | `POST /v1/files` → pass its `key` as `fileKey` to an import endpoint — see [Files](#files)      |
| Answer a sign-in prompt         | poll the task's `login-inputs` list → `PUT` the value                                           |
| Run an accessibility test       | `POST /v1/accessibility/{projectId}` → `GET /v1/accessibility/{projectId}` → read by `reportId` |
| Track keywords                  | `POST /v1/visibility/{projectId}/keyword` → group them → `GET /v1/visibility/{projectId}`       |
| Comment on a sitemap item       | `GET /v1/comments/{projectId}` → read one thread → `POST` → `PATCH` or `DELETE`                 |

### Crawl a website

1. `POST /v1/project/url` submits the crawl and answers `200` with the new project id. The crawl
   runs in the background, so the project exists immediately but has no pages yet.
2. `GET /v1/project/url/{id}` reports progress. Poll it — it answers immediately and costs
   nothing but a request. `status` moves `PENDING` (queued) → `RUNNING` (crawling) → `PERSIST`
   (writing results) → `FINISHED` (done).
3. `GET /v1/project/{projectId}` is readable the whole time, so you can stop polling as soon as
   `status` is `FINISHED` and read the project, its sitemap items (`GET /v1/project/{projectId}/item`)
   and its inventory (`GET /v1/inventory/{projectId}`).

To re-crawl a project that already exists, use `POST /v1/project/url/{id}/refresh`. It answers
immediately and nothing reports its progress, so re-poll `GET /v1/project/url/{id}` for the
project state rather than expecting a refresh status.

### Import a text or XML file

The same shape as a crawl, with its own poll endpoint:

1. `POST /v1/project/text` (one URL per line) or `POST /v1/project/xml` (a sitemap) answers
   `200` with the new project id.
2. `GET /v1/project/text/{id}` or `GET /v1/project/xml/{id}` reports how many URLs have been
   imported. `finished` turns true when the import completes.
3. Read the project with the project endpoints.

Both endpoints accept **one** source: a `file` part (multipart), a `fileKey` from
`POST /v1/files`, or a `url`. Sending none, or more than one, answers `400 invalid_file_source`.
Refreshing an imported project with `POST /v1/project/text/{id}/refresh` only works for projects
created from a URL; a project created by uploading a file cannot be refreshed that way.

### Create an empty project

Use this when the sitemap is going to be built by hand rather than discovered. Nothing is crawled
and nothing is fetched, so the call is finished when it answers:

1. `POST /v1/project/scratch` answers `201` with the new project id. The whole body is optional:
   `{"title": "Marketing site"}` names the project, and leaving it out calls it `Untitled Project`.
2. The project arrives published and complete, with one page: a root item titled `Home` at
   `https://www.example.com`. That address is a placeholder, not a page that was fetched, and it is
   also the project's `domain` and its placeholder image.
3. Build the tree with the item endpoints. `PATCH /v1/project/{projectId}/item/{itemId}` renames
   and re-addresses the root — which also rewrites the project's domain — `POST
   /v1/project/{projectId}/item` adds pages beneath it, and `PUT
   /v1/project/{projectId}/item/{itemId}/content` fills one.

There is no job to poll, unlike the four endpoints that populate a project from outside. The
project counts against the plan's project allowance, and at the allowance the call answers `400
project_limit_reached`.

### Answer a sign-in prompt

A crawl of a site behind a login, and an accessibility run on one, can stop and ask for a value —
an MFA code, for example. The work stays `RUNNING` while it waits.

1. Poll the list for your task: `GET /v1/project/{projectId}/login-inputs` for a crawl,
   `GET /v1/accessibility/{projectId}/{reportId}/login-inputs` for an accessibility run.
2. When an item reports `ready: 1`, send its value with the matching `PUT`.
3. Send an empty object — no `value` — when the prompt only needs to be acknowledged, such as an
   authenticator approval where the run reports the number to match. The value the run filled in
   is kept.

A prompt that expires is reported as completed rather than disappearing, so an id never comes to
mean a different prompt.

### Run an accessibility test

1. `POST /v1/accessibility/{projectId}` starts a run and answers `200`.
2. `GET /v1/accessibility/{projectId}` lists the runs. **The `id` of a row is the `reportId`**
   every other accessibility endpoint takes.
3. Read the run: `GET /v1/accessibility/{projectId}/{reportId}` for its pages,
   `/problems` for the issues by severity, `/groups` for the WCAG structure, and
   `/{reportId}/{itemId}` for one page's result.

`DELETE /v1/accessibility/{projectId}/{reportId}` deletes one run, not every result for the project.

### Track keywords

1. `GET /v1/visibility/locales` lists the values `locale` accepts.
2. `POST /v1/visibility/{projectId}/keyword` adds keywords and answers their ids.
3. `POST /v1/visibility/{projectId}/group` creates a group, then
   `PATCH /v1/visibility/{projectId}/keyword-group` assigns keywords to it, and
   `PATCH /v1/visibility/{projectId}/keyword-setting` sets their locale and device.
4. `GET /v1/visibility/{projectId}` lists the keywords and their positions, filterable by
   `groupId`, `locale` and `device`. `GET /v1/visibility/{projectId}/score` aggregates them.

### Comment on a sitemap item

1. `GET /v1/comments/{projectId}` lists the items that carry comments, most recently commented
   first. Items with no comments are not listed, and neither are items that have been deleted from
   the sitemap.
2. `GET /v1/comments/{projectId}/{itemId}` reads one item's thread, oldest first, paged and
   searchable. `GET /v1/comments/{projectId}/all` reads the whole project newest first — the
   moderation view — with each row naming its item.
3. `POST /v1/comments/{projectId}/{itemId}` publishes a comment and answers `201` with it. The
   commenter is the user the token belongs to: there is no way to post as somebody else, and no
   approval step — the comment is visible immediately.
4. `PATCH /v1/comments/{projectId}/{itemId}/{commentId}` rewrites the text; `DELETE` on the same
   path removes it. Deleting is a **soft** delete: the comment stops appearing everywhere, the row
   is kept, and repeating the call answers `204` again. There is no restore through the API.

Three rules are worth knowing before you write. Any user who can reach the project may edit or
delete any comment on it, including somebody else's — that is how the application's own comment
screens work, and it is team moderation rather than an oversight. A comment is 1 to 1000
characters after trimming, on an edit as well as on a post. And writes are refused on a project
that is not published, and on an item that has been deleted from the sitemap, so an id from
another project cannot be written to.

## Conventions

Shared by most endpoints, and worth reading once.

### Paging

List endpoints take `page` (1-based, default 1) and `limit`, and answer four fields: `total`
(every match, before the page is cut), `page`, `limit`, and `pageSize` — which is the **number of
pages** `total` divides into, not the number of rows returned. Keep requesting pages until you
have collected `total` rows.

### Dates

Dates and times are ISO 8601. Analytics endpoints take `startDate` and `endDate` as `YYYY-MM-DD`,
and both are required. Ranges are inclusive at both ends.

### Where the IDs come from

| ID in a path | Produced by                                                       |
| :----------- | :---------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `projectId`  | the create endpoints, and `id` on each row from `GET /v1/project` |
| `itemId`     | `GET /v1/project/{projectId}/item`                                |
| `reportId`   | `GET /v1/accessibility/{projectId}`                               |
| `keywordId`  | `GET /v1/visibility/{projectId}`                                  |
| `fileKey`    | `POST /v1/files`                                                  |

IDs are scoped to the account and the project that owns them, so another account's id is never
readable. Endpoints do not all report that the same way; see [Known issues](#known-issues).

## Errors

Two bodies are possible, and the same key carries different things in each. Check the status code
before you read `error`.

A **thrown error** (`400`, `404`, `409`, `413`, `429`, `500`) repeats the status and puts the
machine-readable code in `code`:

```json
{
  "statusCode": 404,
  "error": "Not Found",
  "message": "Project not found",
  "code": "project_not_found"
}
```

A **refusal from a guard** (`401`, `403`) puts the machine-readable code in `error`, and there is no
`statusCode`:

```json
{
  "error": "invalid_token",
  "message": "Access token expired"
}
```

Branch on `code` where it exists and on `error` for `401` and `403` — never on `message`, which is
prose and may be reworded.

The codes you are most likely to handle:

| `code`                | Status | When                                                                                     |
| :-------------------- | :----- | :--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `invalid_request`     | `401`  | The `Authorization` header is missing or is not a bearer token.                          |
| `invalid_token`       | `401`  | The token is malformed, expired or was revoked. Get a new one.                           |
| `unauthorized_access` | `403`  | The token is valid but the caller may not read this project.                             |
| `feature_disabled`    | `403`  | The account's plan does not include the feature behind the call. Retrying will not help. |
| `project_not_found`   | `404`  | No project with that id is visible to this account.                                      |
| `file_too_large`      | `413`  | The upload exceeds 64 MB, or exceeds a limit enforced while it is read.                  |
| `FST_ERR_VALIDATION`  | `400`  | The body, query or a path id failed validation. `message` names the field that failed.   |

A `code` is not sent on `401` or `403` — their `error` field is the code — and not on `429`.

**5xx** are not something to handle per code: they mean the request did not complete. See
[Known issues](#known-issues) for the cases where a precondition failure answers `500`.

## Rate limits

Every request is counted against the credential that authenticated it. By default a credential may
make **600 requests in 60 seconds**, and the window starts again at the top of each minute.

- A **Personal Access Token** has its own allowance.
- Every **OAuth 2.0 access token** issued to one application shares that application's allowance,
  and refreshing an access token does not reset it.

The current allowance is reported on every limited response:

| Header                | Description                                               |
| :-------------------- | :-------------------------------------------------------- |
| `RateLimit-Limit`     | Requests allowed in the current window.                   |
| `RateLimit-Remaining` | Requests left in the current window.                      |
| `RateLimit-Reset`     | Seconds until the window ends and the count starts again. |

When the allowance is used up, the request is answered with `429 Too Many Requests`, a `Retry-After`
header in seconds, and a body naming the error code:

```json
{
  "statusCode": 429,
  "error": "Too Many Requests",
  "message": "Rate limit exceeded for this API key. Retry in 12 seconds."
}
```

The `429` body carries no `code`: read the status, and wait for `Retry-After` seconds before trying
again.

Requests that are rejected count too, so retrying while throttled uses up the next window rather
than earning free attempts. The work behind the API — crawling a project, running an audit — is
queued and answers immediately, so a client that waits for results instead of polling in a tight
loop rarely comes close to the limit.

## Files

Some endpoints take a file as their input. Instead of sending that file with every request, upload
it once and pass the **key** you get back.

### 1. Upload the file

`POST /v1/files` takes a `purpose` and the file itself, and answers `201` with the key.

```bash
curl -X POST https://api.dynomapper.com/v1/files \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer ACCESS_TOKEN" \
  -F purpose=project_xml \
  -F file=@sitemap.xml
```

```json
{
  "key": "uploads/api/project_xml/q/4d2f8c1e-8f3b-4c47-9a5e-2b7d0e6c9f11/sitemap.xml",
  "name": "sitemap.xml",
  "size": 20480,
  "mimeType": "application/xml"
}
```

`purpose` says what the file is for. The type and the 64 MB limit are checked against it, and only
an endpoint that asks for the same purpose accepts the key:

| Purpose        | Used by                 | Accepted types                                                      |
| :------------- | :---------------------- | :------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| `project_text` | `POST /v1/project/text` | `text/*`, `application/json`, `application/xml`, `application/yaml` |
| `project_xml`  | `POST /v1/project/xml`  | `text/plain`, `text/xml`, `application/xml`                         |

### 2. Use the key

Pass the key as `fileKey`: at the top level of a JSON body, or inside `body` when the request is
multipart. This is what makes the key worth having: the request no longer carries the file.

```bash
curl -X POST https://api.dynomapper.com/v1/project/xml \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer ACCESS_TOKEN" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"fileKey": "uploads/api/project_xml/q/4d2f8c1e-8f3b-4c47-9a5e-2b7d0e6c9f11/sitemap.xml", "speed": "slower"}'
```

The same endpoints still accept a multipart upload (`file`, plus `body` holding the options as
JSON) and a `body.url`, so nothing that worked before has to change. A request names **one** source
— a `fileKey`, a `file` or a `url` — and may send `speed` with it. Sending a `fileKey` together with
a `file` or a `url` is refused with `400 invalid_file_source` rather than one of them being chosen
for you.

A key belongs to the account that uploaded it and can be reused for as many imports as you need. It
is not a public link: the stored object is private, and it is copied into the project's own storage
only when an import adopts it. Uploads wait in a temporary bucket of their own, which is why a key
is the only way to read one back and why an unused upload can expire on its own schedule.

### File errors

| Code                  | Status | When                                                                     |
| :-------------------- | :----- | :----------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `file_required`       | `400`  | `POST /v1/files` was sent without a file.                                |
| `file_empty`          | `400`  | The file has no content.                                                 |
| `invalid_file_type`   | `400`  | The file's type is not accepted for the purpose.                         |
| `file_too_large`      | `413`  | The file is larger than 64 MB.                                           |
| `invalid_file_source` | `400`  | The import request named no source, or more than one.                    |
| `file_not_found`      | `404`  | The key does not exist, belongs to another account, or is malformed.     |
| `purpose_mismatch`    | `400`  | The key was uploaded for a different purpose than the endpoint asks for. |

A malformed key and a key belonging to another account answer the same `404`, so the endpoint
cannot be used to discover keys.

## Known issues

Tracked defects in the API rather than intended design, documented so a client does not have to
discover them at runtime. Each is expected to change; the workaround keeps working after it does.

1. **Some precondition failures answer `500` instead of a 4xx.** These all mean "the request cannot
   be applied in the project's current state", but they are raised as internal errors:
   - `DELETE /v1/project/url/{id}` when the crawl has already started or the project is published —
     `Project is not in cancellable state`.
   - `DELETE /v1/project/url/{id}/refresh` when nothing is outstanding —
     `No outstanding refresh found for project ID {id}`. Treat this as "nothing to cancel".
   - `POST /v1/project/text/{id}/refresh` and its XML twin when the project was not created from a
     URL.
   - `GET /v1/inventory/{projectId}/summary` when the project has no crawl statistics yet.
   - `GET /v1/project/{projectId}/item/{itemId}` for an item id that is not in the project.

2. **A refresh job id is not exposed.** `POST /v1/project/url` returns the crawler's `jobId` for
   the crawl it started, but `POST /v1/project/url/{id}/refresh` produces a refresh id and a job id
   that its response does not carry — it answers with the project id and any login prompts. Track a
   refresh through the project: `GET /v1/project/url/{id}` reports the project, not the job.

3. **Several path ids are not validated.** A non-numeric `projectId`, `itemId`, `reportId` or
   `linkId` on those routes fails inside the handler and answers `500` rather than `400`. Validate
   ids before sending them.

4. **Creation endpoints disagree on the status code.** `POST /v1/project/url`, `POST
   /v1/project/text` and `POST /v1/project/xml` answer `200` with the new project id;
   `POST /v1/project/scratch`, `POST /v1/files` and `POST /v1/comments/{projectId}/{itemId}` answer
   `201`. Nothing depends on the difference — no endpoint sends a `Location` header, and the id is
   in the body either way — so read the body rather than the status.

get.description:
Returns the user the access token belongs to, and the account that user works in. This is the cheapest way to check that a token works: it reads no project and needs no id, so it is the call to make first when a request fails and you want to know whether the credential or the request is at fault.

`accountId` is what the rest of the API is scoped to — every project, keyword and report belongs to an account rather than to a user. `thirdPartyProviders` lists the external identities linked for signing in, which matters only if your integration also signs users in through the application.

200.description: The user the token belongs to, and the account they work in.

id.description: ID of the authenticated user.

accountId.description: ID of the account the user works in. Every project and report in the API belongs to an account rather than to a user, so this is the id shared with the account’s other members.

email.description: Email address the user signs in with.

name.description: Display name the user chose in the application. An empty string when the user has not set one, never `null`.

company.description: Company recorded on the user’s profile. An empty string when unset, never `null`.

get.description:
Lists the projects this account can read, one row per project, newest crawl first unless `order` says otherwise. Only published projects are listed by default: a project whose first crawl is still running is reachable by id through `GET /v1/project/{projectId}` but does not appear here. Pass `filter=archived` to list archived projects instead.

`items` on each row is the count stored on the project, not a recount taken for this response. `group` takes an id from `GET /v1/project/group` and `-1` for ungrouped projects, `search` matches the title, and `limit` must be between 10 and 100 while `page` is 1-based — `total` is the number of projects matching the filters across every page.

Projects are created by `POST /v1/project/url`, `POST /v1/project/text`, `POST /v1/project/xml` or `POST /v1/project/sharepoint`, and read one at a time through `GET /v1/project/{projectId}`. The categories, workflow statuses and groups used elsewhere in the API come from `GET /v1/project/category`, `GET /v1/project/workflow-status` and `GET /v1/project/group`.

parameters.name: page
parameters.description: Page of results to return, 1-based. Defaults to 1, and the page size is `limit`, so the last page is `total` divided by `limit` rounded up.

parameters.name: search
parameters.description: Text to match anywhere in the project title; surrounding whitespace is trimmed before the match. Omit it to list projects regardless of title.

parameters.name: order
parameters.description: Sort order. `latest` (the default) is most recently crawled first, `oldest` the reverse of that, `title` sorts alphabetically, `items` puts the projects with the most items first, and `latest_modified` / `oldest_modified` sort by when the project record was last changed.

parameters.name: filter
parameters.description: Which projects to list. `none` (the default) lists published projects only; `scheduled` narrows that to projects with a weekly or monthly crawl schedule; `archived` lists archived projects and nothing else.

parameters.name: group
parameters.description: Project group to list, using an id from GET /v1/project/group. Pass -1 to list only projects that are in no group. Omit it — or send 0 — to list grouped and ungrouped projects together.

parameters.name: limit
parameters.description: Page size. Minimum 10, maximum 100, default 100. A value outside the range is rejected with 400.

200.description: A page of projects, with the total number matching the filters.

total.description: Number of projects matching the filters, across every page — not the number of rows in `items`.

limit.description: Page size this response was built with: `limit` from the request, or the default of 100.

page.description: Page number this response holds: `page` from the request, or the default of 1.

alphaId.description: Opaque alphanumeric id the application uses in its own URLs, such as `sitemapUrl`. It encodes the same project as `id`, and this API never accepts it in place of `id`.

type.description: How the project was created. `crawler` is a crawl of a website (POST /v1/project/url or POST /v1/project/sharepoint), `text` an imported text list of URLs (POST /v1/project/text), `xml` an imported XML sitemap (POST /v1/project/xml). `scratch` is a project built by hand in the application, `duplicate` one copied from another project, and `merge` one combined from several; no endpoint here creates those three.

items.description: Item count stored on the project row — the figure the application’s project list shows. It is a saved count rather than one taken for this response, so it is not guaranteed to match the pages and folders currently in the sitemap.

isPublic.description: True when the project’s share record is public. It is stored separately from `isPrivate`, so the two flags can disagree.

isPrivate.description: Private project: not publicly reachable. Every project created by POST /v1/project/sharepoint is stored private.

get.description:
Returns one project, with the counts and flags that decide what can be done with it. Three different numbers are reported: `items` is the item count stored on the project, `pages` is the number of published pages counted now, and `buckets` the number of published containers — the folders that group pages. The stored count is not guaranteed to be the sum of the other two.

A project is readable while its first crawl is still running: it is pending, and `crawlDate` reports its creation date until that crawl finishes. Deleted, unpublished and archived projects answer 404, and so does a project belonging to another account. `allowTextRefresh` and `allowXmlRefresh` say whether `POST /v1/project/text/{id}/refresh` and `POST /v1/project/xml/{id}/refresh` will accept this project.

This is the read to make once the work behind a project has finished. Progress is reported elsewhere: `GET /v1/project/url/{id}` for a crawl, `GET /v1/project/text/{id}` and `GET /v1/project/xml/{id}` for imports, and `GET /v1/project/{projectId}/vacq` or `GET /v1/project/{projectId}/dacq` for its scores.

get.description:
Returns the VACQ score of a project that is publicly reachable: content quality, accessibility and search visibility, plus their average. A private SharePoint project has no search visibility to measure and is scored with DACQ instead — read `GET /v1/project/{projectId}/dacq` for those.

The pillars are measured by other families, so each can be missing on its own: accessibility needs a completed accessibility run (`POST /v1/accessibility/{projectId}`) and visibility needs keywords tracked for the project’s domain (`POST /v1/visibility/{projectId}/keyword`). A pillar that has not been measured is null, and `average` stays null until all three are available, so a project that has only been crawled answers nulls rather than zeros.

The project is resolved before this handler runs, which is also why an id that is not readable answers 404 or 403 rather than a scored body.

parameters.name: projectId
parameters.description: Project id: the value returned by the create endpoints, and the `id` of each row from `GET /v1/project`.

200.description: The three VACQ pillars and their average, null where a pillar has not been measured.

average.description: VACQ total: the mean of the three pillars, rounded to two decimals. Null unless content quality, accessibility and visibility are all measured, the accessibility score is above zero, and the account tracks at least one active keyword for the project’s domain.

accessibility.description: Accessibility pillar: the percentage score of the project’s most recent accessibility run, started with POST /v1/accessibility/{projectId}. Null when no run has produced a score.

contentQuality.description: Content quality pillar: a percentage computed from the crawl’s total and unique link counts as `(total − unique) / total × 100`, with the orphaned-page share contributing up to nine percent. Null when the project has no crawl statistics. The DACQ endpoint reports the same base figure without the orphan adjustment.

visibility.description: Visibility pillar: the Google visibility score of the project’s domain over the last 30 days, from the ranking data the account tracks for its keywords. Null when the account tracks no keyword for this domain.

get.description:
Get the DACQ score of a private SharePoint project.

DACQ replaces VACQ for projects that are not publicly reachable: with no search visibility to measure, the total is built from Discoverability, Accessibility and Content Quality instead.

The average is `null` until all three pillars are measured. Discoverability comes from the crawl; Accessibility needs a completed accessibility run — start one with `POST /v1/accessibility/{projectId}`. Authenticated projects can pause for a deferred input (an MFA code, for example) during that run.

Projects that are not private SharePoint projects, and projects that have not been crawled yet, return every field as null rather than a 404.

get.description:
The categories the account uses to label sitemap pages, in the order the application shows them. Hidden categories are left out, so this is the set a client can actually assign.

Categories are reported flat: the application can nest one under another, and this list carries the order only, not the nesting, so a nested category is listed where its position puts it.

An `id` here is what `GET /v1/project/{projectId}/item` reports as an item’s `category`, and what `GET /v1/assignments` accepts as its `category` filter. Categories are not a parameter of the project list.

A category with `editable: false` is one every account shares. It can be recoloured and moved, and it can be hidden with `DELETE /v1/project/category/{categoryId}`, but it cannot be renamed or deleted — the write endpoints refuse them with 409. A `color` of null means no color is set.

color.description: Color the application paints the category with, when one is set. Null when the category has no color.

editable.description: False for a category every account shares: its name cannot be changed and it cannot be deleted, only recoloured and hidden. True for a category this account created.

items.description: The account’s visible categories, in the order the application lists them.

post.description:
Makes sure a category of this name is visible to the account, and answers it. The name is trimmed and compared exactly, so `Landing page` and `landing page` are two categories — and it is compared against names, not ids, because a name is how the application itself looks a category up.

This is an ensure rather than a plain create, which is what makes it safe to repeat: a name that is already visible answers the existing category and writes nothing. Otherwise four rows are tried in order — the account’s own visible category, the shared one, the account’s own category that a delete soft-deleted earlier (which is revived), and only then a new row. A name whose only match is hidden for this account comes back visible: adding it again is how the application un-hides it.

A new category is appended to the end of the list. A revived one keeps the place it had before it was deleted. The response is the category as `GET /v1/project/category` reports it, and it answers 200 rather than 201 because the call may have revived a row instead of creating one.

Duplicate names are allowed. The application never enforced uniqueness, so two categories may share one, and the call will answer whichever of them is visible first — the account’s own before a shared one, then the lowest id.

patch.description:
Renames a category, sets or clears its color, or both. Only the keys you send are written, so sending `name` alone leaves the color alone; `color: null` removes a color.

Color is stored per account, including for a category every account shares: recolouring one changes what this account sees and nothing else. Renaming a shared category is refused with 409, because the row is every other account’s category too — to have one of your own with that name, create it with `POST /v1/project/category`.

Renaming does not touch the items that carry the category: an item stores the id, so it follows the new name automatically. Sending neither field answers 400 with `nothing_to_update`, because there would be nothing to do.

The response is the category as `GET /v1/project/category` reports it.

delete.description:
Takes the category out of this account’s list. A category the account created is soft-deleted, so `POST /v1/project/category` with the same name revives it later with its old place in the list. A category every account shares cannot be deleted at all, so it is hidden for this account instead — the same thing the application’s own delete does.

Items are not touched. A page keeps the `category` value it carried, which is why a project that was filtered by this category still answers what it always did; the category no longer appears as a choice. That mirrors the application, where deleting a category is a list decision rather than a migration.

The call is idempotent: repeating it answers the same `200` and writes nothing the second time. The response is the id that was removed rather than the row, because after the call the row is no longer part of the list.

post.description:
Places a category directly after another one in the account’s list, or first when `afterId` is null. The list is the one `GET /v1/project/category` returns, so a hidden category is not a position anything can be moved to.

The whole list is renumbered from 1 as part of the move. The application orders categories by that number alone, so a gap or a duplicate would put a category somewhere neither the caller nor the application asked for — renumbering is what keeps "after this one" true after the next move as well.

Answers the category that was moved, as `GET /v1/project/category` reports it.

parameters.name: categoryId
parameters.description: ID of the category, as `GET /v1/project/category` reports it.

200.description: The category after the move, in the shape the list returns.

get.description:
The statuses a sitemap page can be given, in the order the application offers them. The ten built-in statuses — `draft`, `publish`, `pending`, `complete`, `incomplete`, `action`, `leaveasis`, `improve`, `consolidate` and `remove` — exist for every account without being stored, and each is listed unless the account has hidden it, so a list can hold fewer than ten. Statuses the account created appear alongside them, and a status with a parent is listed after the statuses without one. Within each group the order is the account’s own. Hidden statuses are left out.

`key` is what a sitemap item reports as `workflowStatus` (see `GET /v1/project/{projectId}/item`) and the value to send as the `workflow` filter of `GET /v1/assignments`. Built-in statuses use their key as their `id`; statuses the account created have a numeric id. The write endpoints address a status by its `key`, so a key containing `#` — `wfs#12`, which is what a nested status gets — has to be percent-encoded as `wfs%2312` when it appears in a path.

A status with `editable: false` is one of the built-in ten. It can be recoloured, reordered and hidden, but not renamed, deleted or nested — the write endpoints refuse them with 409. A `color` of null means no color is set.

200.description: The account’s workflow statuses, in the order the application offers them.

id.description: Identifier of the status: the key itself for a built-in status, a numeric id for one the account created.

key.description: Stable key of the status, for example `publish`. This is the value an item carries in `workflowStatus`, the value to send as the `workflow` filter of GET /v1/assignments, and the path parameter of the status write endpoints. A status the account created may be keyed `wfs#12`; where such a key goes in a path it has to be percent-encoded (`wfs%2312`), because a bare `#` starts a fragment.

name.description: Name the application shows for the status.

parentKey.description: Key of the parent status when this one is nested under another in the application’s menu. Null for a top-level status.

color.description: Color the application paints the status with. Null when the status has no color.

editable.description: False for one of the ten built-in statuses: it can be recoloured, reordered and hidden, but not renamed, deleted or nested. True for a status this account created.

items.description: The visible workflow statuses, built-in ones first and each nested status after its parent.

post.description:
Makes sure a workflow status of this name is visible to the account, and answers it. The key is derived from the name the way the application derives it — lowercased, with each space replaced by an underscore — because the key, not the id, is what every item stores.

This is an ensure rather than a plain create, which is what makes it safe to repeat. A name that resolves to one of the ten built-in keys answers that built-in and un-hides it if the account had hidden it: a status called `Draft` is the application’s Draft, not a second one. Otherwise the account’s own visible status with that key or name answers the call, then one a delete soft-deleted earlier (which is revived), and only then is a row created.

A name longer than twenty characters cannot be its own key — the column is that wide — so the new status is stored under `wfs#<id>` instead, as is one created with a parent. That is the key items will carry, and the key to use in the path of the other write endpoints — sent as `wfs%23<id>` there, because the `#` is a fragment marker in a URL. A new status is appended to the end of its list; a revived one keeps the place it had.

Sending `parentKey` is the one case that always writes a row, nested one level under that status and keyed `wfs#<id>`. That is how the application nests a status, and looking the name up instead would put it at the root. A key in a body is plain text, so `parentKey` takes `wfs#12` as it is — only a key in a path needs the percent sign. Duplicate names are allowed: the application never enforced uniqueness, so two statuses may share one name as long as their keys differ.

The response is the status as `GET /v1/project/workflow-status` reports it, and it answers 200 rather than 201 because the call may have revived a row instead of creating one.

name.description: Name of the status. Trimmed; 1 to 255 characters. Its key is derived from it, and a status with that key or name is returned if one already exists.

parentKey.description: Key of the status to nest the new one under. Omit it, or send null, for a top-level status. A status can only be nested one level deep.

200.description: The status with this name, after the write.

id.description: Identifier of the status: the key itself for a built-in status, a numeric id for one the account created.

key.description: Stable key of the status, for example `publish`. A status the account created may be keyed `wfs#12`; where such a key goes in a path it has to be percent-encoded (`wfs%2312`), because a bare `#` starts a fragment.

patch.description:
Renames a status the account created, sets or clears the color of any status including a built-in one, or both. Only the keys you send are written, so sending `name` alone leaves the color alone; `color: null` removes a color.

Renaming does not change the key. That is deliberate and it is what the application does: every item stores the key, so re-deriving it from the new name would silently orphan every page carrying the status. The key in the path is therefore still the key afterwards — only the `name` moves.

A built-in status cannot be renamed, because its name is part of the application rather than of the account; that answers 409. It can be recoloured. Sending neither field answers 400 with `nothing_to_update`.

The response is the status as `GET /v1/project/workflow-status` reports it.

Takes the status out of this account’s list. A status the account created is soft-deleted, so `POST /v1/project/workflow-status` with the same name revives it later with its old place in the list. A built-in status cannot be deleted at all, so it is hidden for this account instead — the same thing the application’s own delete does.

Items are not touched: a page keeps the `workflowStatus` it carried, which is why a project filtered by this status still answers what it always did, even though the status is no longer offered as a choice. Statuses nested under this one are left where they are, as the application leaves them — they keep a parent that is no longer listed, and moving them is a move of your own.

The call is idempotent: repeating it answers the same `200` and writes nothing the second time. The response is the key that was removed rather than the row, because after the call the row is no longer part of the list.

post.description:
Reorders a status within its list, moves it under another status, or lifts it back to the top level. `parentKey` names the list to move into — omit it, or send null, for the top level — and `afterKey` the position inside that list, with null meaning first. Both are body values, so a key such as `wfs#12` is sent as it is; only the `key` in the path is percent-encoded.

Statuses are one level deep, so three moves are refused: nesting a status that is already nested, nesting one that has children (both `parent_too_deep`), and naming the status as its own parent (`parent_cycle`). With one level those are the only cycles there are. A built-in status can be reordered but not nested, which answers 409; its position at the top level is the application’s, not the account’s.

Every list the move touches is renumbered from 1. The application sorts each list by that number alone, so a gap would put the row somewhere neither the caller nor the application asked for.

Answers the status that was moved, as `GET /v1/project/workflow-status` reports it.

afterKey.description: Key of the status to place this one after, inside the list named by `parentKey`. Null puts it first in that list.

parameters.description: Key of the status, exactly as `GET /v1/project/workflow-status` reports it: a built-in key is a plain word such as `publish`, and one the account created may be `wfs#12`. A `#` in a path starts a fragment, so that key has to be sent percent-encoded as `wfs%2312` — sent as `wfs#12`, everything from the `#` is dropped before the request leaves the client and nothing reaches this route.

A status the account created may be keyed `wfs#12`; where such a key goes in a path it has to be percent-encoded (`wfs%2312`), because a bare `#` starts a fragment.

parentKey.description: Key of the parent status when this one is nested under another in the application’s menu. Null for a top-level status.

get.description:
Lists the sitemap tree of a project, one row per item, so a client can walk the project the way the application’s sitemap editor does. An item is either a page (`type: link`) or a container that groups pages (`type: container`); `url` is the page’s address and `children` the number of published items beneath it. The counts cover published items and comments only.

Send `parentId` to list one item’s part of the tree instead of the whole tree: the item itself comes first, followed by every published item beneath it, with `depth` counted from that item. The rows are a subtree, not only the direct children — a page has none, so it returns itself. `limit` and `offset` page the result: `offset` is 0-based and is only applied when `limit` is sent, and when both are sent `nextOffset` is `offset + limit`, ready to be requested next. Without `limit` every matching item is returned and `nextOffset` is null. `total` counts all items under `parentId` regardless of paging.

The tree is cut at the project’s configured maximum level, so the rows are the upper part of the tree rather than every item ever recorded, and `total` can be larger than the number of rows. `depth` is the level the tree records for the row: a position in the tree rather than a count of link hops from the start URL. To read one item with its metadata, use `GET /v1/project/{projectId}/item/{itemId}`.

parameters.name: parentId
parameters.description: ID of the item to list from: its subtree is returned, the item itself first (`depth: 0`) when it is published. Omit it to list from the top of the sitemap. An id that is not in this project lists nothing rather than failing.

parameters.name: limit
parameters.description: Maximum number of items to return. Omit it to return every matching item; the API applies no default and no maximum.

parameters.name: offset
parameters.description: Number of items to skip, 0-based. Only applied when `limit` is also sent; without `limit` the whole set is returned from the beginning.

parameters.name: projectId
parameters.description: Project id: the value returned by the create endpoints, and the `id` of each row from `GET /v1/project`.

200.description: One page of the sitemap tree, with the offsets needed to ask for the next.

parentId.description: Item the listing was made from: `parentId` from the request, or null when the whole tree was listed.

total.description: Number of items the listing covers, across every page — not the number of rows in `items`. It includes the item named by `parentId`, and it can be larger than the rows even without paging, because the tree is cut at the project’s maximum level.

limit.description: Page size the request used, or null when `limit` was omitted and everything was returned.

offset.description: Number of items skipped before the first row, or null when the request sent no `offset`.

nextOffset.description: Offset to send for the next page: `offset + limit`. It is computed without checking whether more items exist, so a page shorter than `limit` means there is nothing left. Null when `offset` or `limit` was omitted.

id.description: Item id. Read the item through GET /v1/project/{projectId}/item/{itemId}, and use it in `includeLinksByProject` or `excludeLinksByProject` when creating a crawl with POST /v1/project/url.

title.description: Title of the page or container, as the application stores it.

url.description: Address of the page this item represents. Null when the item has no address of its own, as a container normally does not.

type.description: What the item is. `link` is a page with a URL; `container` is a folder that groups other items and is not itself a page.

category.description: ID of the category assigned to the item, from GET /v1/project/category. Null when it is uncategorised.

workflowStatus.description: Workflow status assigned to the item, as the key returned by GET /v1/project/workflow-status, for example `publish`. Null when no status is set.

parent.description: ID of the item’s parent in the sitemap tree. 0 when the item sits at the root.

ordering.description: Order index the application uses to sort items within their parent.

depth.description: Level the sitemap tree records for the row: its position in the tree rather than a count of link hops from the start URL.

children.description: Number of published items the application counts beneath this one.

comments.description: Number of published comments recorded for the item’s page.

contentCount.description: Number of content blocks the page holds, as the application counts them. 0 for a container, and for a page whose content has not been crawled or written yet. Read the blocks themselves through GET /v1/project/{projectId}/item/{itemId}/content.

linkStatus.description: Link status the crawler recorded for the item, in the application’s own encoding. Null when the item has no recorded status.

linkType.description: Link type the crawler recorded for the item, in the application’s own encoding. Null when it has none.

backgroundColor.description: Background color the application paints the item with in the sitemap. Null when it uses the default.

foregroundColor.description: Text color the application paints the item with in the sitemap. Null when it uses the default.

items.description: The items on this page.

post.description:
Adds an item to the project’s sitemap tree: a page when `url` is sent, a container when it is not. The item is published immediately, carries no children, and takes its place after `afterItemId` or at the end of its parent’s children. Send neither `parentId` nor a sibling id to create the root item; a project has exactly one, so once it has one this answers `root_exists`.

`category` and `workflowStatus` are ids, not names: pass a value from `GET /v1/project/category` or `GET /v1/project/workflow-status`. An unknown value is rejected rather than created, so a typo cannot silently add a category to the account.

The write is recorded in the project’s undo history, so `POST /v1/project/{projectId}/item/history/undo` reverses it — and the application’s own Undo button reverses it too. The response is the new item, in the same shape `GET /v1/project/{projectId}/item/{itemId}` returns.

`pathMode` is the one field the response reports separately, because the address is not always saved with the item. The item is created either way: `linkPathSaved` answers `true` when the address was saved and `false` when it was not, and sending `PATCH /v1/project/{projectId}/item/{itemId}` with `pathMode` again retries it.

title.description: Title of the new item. Required; the editor’s form requires one too.

url.description: Address the item points at, stored verbatim — no trimming, no validation, no de-duplication, so two items may share one URL. Sending `null` or an empty string turns the item into a container; sending a URL turns it into a link and records the URL’s MD5 for the application’s own lookups.

category.description: ID of the category to assign, from `GET /v1/project/category`. `null` clears it. An id this account cannot see is rejected with `unknown_category`; categories are never created implicitly.

workflowStatus.description: Workflow status key to assign, from `GET /v1/project/workflow-status`, for example `publish`. `null` clears it. An unknown key is rejected with `unknown_workflow_status`; statuses are never created implicitly.

priority.description: Sitemap priority, between 0 and 1 inclusive. New items default to 0.5, the value the editor uses.

changeFrequency.description: How often the page is expected to change, as a sitemap change frequency. `null` clears it. Only these seven values are accepted, unlike the free-text field the editor’s form allows.

metaDescription.description: Meta description of the page. `null` clears it.

metaKeywords.description: Meta keywords of the page. `null` clears it.

backgroundColor.description: Background color the application paints the item with in the sitemap. `null` restores the default.

foregroundColor.description: Text color the application paints the item with in the sitemap. `null` restores the default.

tags.description: Tags of the item, as the complete set: the array replaces the tags the item has, in the order given, and duplicates are dropped. Send an empty array to remove them all.

hreflang.description: Language alternates of the page, as the complete set: the array replaces the ones recorded. Send an empty array to remove them all.

href.description: Address of the page in that language.

patch.summary: Assign a category, status, tags or colors to sitemap items
patch.description:
Sets one or more attributes across many items in one call — the bulk operations the editor uses when several nodes are selected at once. Send at least one of `category`, `workflowStatus`, `tags` and `colors`; a request that names none is rejected with `nothing_to_update`.

`apply` decides how far each change reaches from the named items: `selected` for the items alone, `children` to include their direct children, `subtree` to include everything beneath them. It is the application’s own selection rule, and it expands server-side, so you do not need to walk the tree yourself. A selection that reaches an item which has been deleted leaves it alone: it was not named, and nothing displays it.

An item that has been deleted cannot be named in `itemIds` at all — the whole request answers `404 item_not_found` and changes nothing.

The batch is capped at 500 ids and it is recorded as one step per attribute in the undo history — a request that sets both a category and tags undoes as two steps, matching what the editor records when it makes those two calls.

itemIds.description: IDs the edit names, at most 500. Every id must belong to this project, otherwise the request is rejected with `invalid_item_ids` and nothing is changed; an id that has been deleted answers `404 item_not_found`.

apply.description: How far the edit reaches from each named id. `selected` (the default) changes only the named items; `children` also changes their direct children; `subtree` changes everything beneath them. The values are the application’s own, and they decide what is written — the undo record keeps only the ids you named, so undoing restores the selection’s values, exactly as the editor would.

category.description: Category id to assign to every affected item, or `null` to clear it. Rejected with `unknown_category` when the account cannot see it.

workflowStatus.description: Workflow status key to assign, or `null` to clear it. Rejected with `unknown_workflow_status` when the key does not exist.

tags.description: Tags to assign. With `tagsMode: replace` this is the complete set for every affected item; with `merge` the tags are added and the items’ other tags stay.

tagsMode.description: What `tags` means. `replace` (the default) makes the array the whole tag set; `merge` adds the tags and keeps the rest.

colors.description: Colors to paint the affected items with, as a pair. Send both keys, or omit the object to leave colors alone.

background.description: Background color, or `null` for the default.

foreground.description: Text color, or `null` for the default.

totalItems.description: Published item count the project reports after the write, as `GET /v1/project/{projectId}` returns it. Deleting or restoring items changes it; moving them does not.

get.description:
Returns one sitemap item with the metadata the sitemap editor shows: the page’s meta keywords and description, its sitemap `priority` and `changeFrequency`, the tags and language alternates recorded for it, and its thumbnail. Metadata falls back to what the crawler recorded for the page when the item itself carries none.

`mode`, `slug` and `staticUrl` describe the public address the application gives the page. When `mode` is `Slug` the address is built from `slug`, when it is `Static` from `staticUrl`, and when it is an empty string neither is meaningful because the application has no link path for the item.

The item is looked up through the project, so a project that cannot be read answers 404 or 403 first. An `itemId` that does not exist in this project, or that is not a number, answers 500 `Item not found` — this API treats that as an illegal state rather than a 404. The paged list of items is `GET /v1/project/{projectId}/item`.

patch.description:
Changes the fields an item carries. Only the keys you send are written, so this is safe to use for a rename as well as for a full edit; sending a key with `null` clears it.

Three consequences are worth knowing before you call it. Sending `url` re-derives the item’s type, so a URL makes it a link and an empty one makes it a container. Editing the URL of a **root** item also rewrites the project’s `domain` from it, and its `image_url` unless the project was crawled — the root item *is* the project’s domain in the application, so editing one edits the other. Sending `tags` or `hreflang` replaces the whole set rather than adding to it.

A title change is recorded as a `renameTitle` step in the undo history, which is what makes the change reversible; the application records nothing for a mixed edit, and reproducing that would leave a `PATCH` that undo could not reach.

The response is the item as `GET /v1/project/{projectId}/item/{itemId}` returns it, plus `linkPathSaved` when `pathMode` was sent. The edit is applied whether or not the address could be saved; `false` says the item now exists without the address you asked for.

An item that has been deleted answers `404 item_not_found`.

title.description: Title of the page or container, shown in the tree and used as the page title. Cannot be empty when it is sent.

url.description: Address the item points at, stored verbatim — no trimming, no validation, no de-duplication, so two items may share one URL. Sending `null` or an empty string turns the item into a container; sending a URL turns it into a link and records the URL’s MD5 for the application’s own lookups.

category.description: ID of the category to assign, from `GET /v1/project/category`. `null` clears it. An id this account cannot see is rejected with `unknown_category`; categories are never created implicitly.

workflowStatus.description: Workflow status key to assign, from `GET /v1/project/workflow-status`, for example `publish`. `null` clears it. An unknown key is rejected with `unknown_workflow_status`; statuses are never created implicitly.

priority.description: Sitemap priority, between 0 and 1 inclusive. New items default to 0.5, the value the editor uses.

changeFrequency.description: How often the page is expected to change, as a sitemap change frequency. `null` clears it. Only these seven values are accepted, unlike the free-text field the editor’s form allows.

metaDescription.description: Meta description of the page. `null` clears it.

metaKeywords.description: Meta keywords of the page. `null` clears it.

backgroundColor.description: Background color the application paints the item with in the sitemap. `null` restores the default.

foregroundColor.description: Text color the application paints the item with in the sitemap. `null` restores the default.

tags.description: Tags of the item, as the complete set: the array replaces the tags the item has, in the order given, and duplicates are dropped. Send an empty array to remove them all.

hreflang.description: Language alternates of the page, as the complete set: the array replaces the ones recorded. Send an empty array to remove them all.

href.description: Address of the page in that language.

pathMode.description: Which address scheme the application should give the page: `Slug` builds the address from `slug`, `Static` uses `staticUrl`. Omit it to leave the item’s link path untouched. There is no way to clear a link path here, matching the editor, which cannot clear one either.

slug.description: Path segment used when `pathMode` is `Slug`. Ignored unless `pathMode` is sent. Defaults to an empty string.

staticUrl.description: Full address served when `pathMode` is `Static`. Ignored unless `pathMode` is sent. Defaults to an empty string.

delete.description:
Deletes an item and everything beneath it. The delete is reversible: `POST /v1/project/{projectId}/item/history/undo` puts the subtree back where it was. Nothing is returned about the descendants — they are deleted with the item, not named in the response.

Deleting an item that is already deleted does nothing and answers the same way, so the call is safe to repeat. The project’s root item cannot be deleted — it is the project’s domain and the top of the tree — so naming it answers `400 root_not_deletable`. The delete is refused on a project that is not published, and it needs a role that may delete items (`sitemap:delete`), which a viewer role does not have.

Because the delete is recorded in the project’s history, the application’s Undo button reverses it and so does this API. To delete several items in one call, use `POST /v1/project/{projectId}/item/delete`.

200.description: The ids the delete covered.

deletedItemIds.description: IDs the request deleted — the named items only, not the descendants that were soft-deleted with them. An item that was already deleted still appears here, so the list always matches the request.

totalItems.description: Published item count the project reports after the delete.

post.description:
Deletes a batch of items, and everything beneath each of them, as one atomic operation: either every id is deleted or none is. An id that is not in this project rejects the whole request with `invalid_item_ids` and the message names the ids that were wrong, rather than deleting the rest.

The batch is capped at 500 ids, and the delete is recorded as one step in the undo history, so undoing it restores the whole batch. Naming the project’s root item rejects the whole request with `root_not_deletable`, since the root is the project’s domain and cannot be deleted. Deleting one item at a time through the call and undoing each would take one step per item; the single-item form is `DELETE /v1/project/{projectId}/item/{itemId}`.

post.description:
Reparents an item, repositions it among its siblings, or both. Omitting `parentId` keeps the current parent and only repositions; sending `null` makes the item a root, which is refused with `root_exists` when the project already has a root, and the root item itself cannot be moved at all (`root_not_movable`); sending a container id moves it under that container. `afterItemId` places it directly after one of its new siblings, and omitting it appends to the end.

The item’s whole subtree moves with it. Its siblings on both sides are renumbered in display order, sharing one sequence with the rows an earlier delete left behind — a deleted item keeps the number it had, so the numbers you see can skip one, and display order is what they encode. A move into the item’s own subtree is refused with `item_cycle` — including a move to itself — rather than corrupting the tree, which is the failure mode the application is exposed to and this API is not.

The move is recorded in the undo history as one step and the response is the item as the item read returns it; its new position is visible by listing the parent’s children with `GET /v1/project/{projectId}/item` and `parentId`. An item that has been deleted answers `404 item_not_found`, and so does a `parentId` that names one. To move several items in one call, use `POST /v1/project/{projectId}/item/move`.

parentId.description: ID of the container to move the item under, or `null` to make it a root item — refused with `root_exists` when the project already has one, which is every project but an empty one. The root item itself cannot be moved at all: naming it answers `root_not_movable`, because at the root it would only reorder a list of one and under a container it would leave the project without its top. Omit `parentId` to keep the current parent. A parent inside the item’s own subtree is rejected with `item_cycle`.

afterItemId.description: ID of the sibling to place the item after, among the published children of `parentId`. Omit it to append to the end.

parameters.name: projectId
parameters.description: Project id: the value returned by the create endpoints, and the `id` of each row from `GET /v1/project`.

parameters.name: itemId
parameters.description: ID of a sitemap item, as returned by `GET /v1/project/{projectId}/item`.

200.description: The item at its new position, in the shape the item read returns.

id.description: Item id.

title.description: Title of the page or container, as the application stores it.

url.description: Address of the page this item represents. Null when the item has no address of its own, as a container normally does not.

type.description: What the item is. `link` is a page with a URL; `container` is a folder that groups other items and is not itself a page.

category.description: ID of the category assigned to the item, from GET /v1/project/category. Null when it is uncategorised.

workflowStatus.description: Workflow status assigned to the item, as the key returned by GET /v1/project/workflow-status, for example `publish`. Null when no status is set.

priority.description: Sitemap priority recorded for the page, as the application stores it. Null when no priority is set.

changeFrequency.description: How often the page is expected to change, as a sitemap change frequency such as `weekly` or `monthly`. The application reports `monthly` when the item has none set.

metaKeywords.description: Meta keywords of the page, taken from the item or from what the crawler recorded for it. Null when neither has them.

metaDescription.description: Meta description of the page, taken from the item or from what the crawler recorded for it. Null when neither has them.

tags.description: Tags attached to the item in the application. Empty when it has none.

thumbnail.description: Thumbnail images recorded for the item. Null when it has none.

title.description: Title recorded for the thumbnail image.

sm.description: Small variant of the thumbnail image, as the application stores it.

lg.description: Large variant of the thumbnail image, as the application stores it.

mode.description: Which address scheme applies to the page. `Slug` means the address is built from `slug`, `Static` that it is `staticUrl`, and an empty string that the application has no link path for the item, so neither field means anything.

slug.description: Path segment the application uses for the page when `mode` is `Slug`. Empty when the application has no link path for the item.

staticUrl.description: Full address the application serves the page at when `mode` is `Static`. Empty when the application has no link path for the item.

backgroundColor.description: Background color the application paints the item with in the sitemap. Null when it uses the default.

foregroundColor.description: Text color the application paints the item with in the sitemap. Null when it uses the default.

href.description: Address of the page in that language, as recorded for the item.

lang.description: Language code of that version, for example `en-US` or `de`.

hreflang.description: Language alternates recorded for the page. Empty when it has none.

post.description:
Moves a batch of items as one atomic operation, all of them or none. The moves are applied in the order given, each resolved against the tree the previous one left, so one call can express a rearrangement that would otherwise take several — and the whole batch undoes as one step.

Every id must belong to this project, every `parentId` must too, no move may name an item that is itself in the batch, and no item may appear twice: a repeated id answers `400 duplicate_item_ids` rather than being applied against the position the first move left. An item that has been deleted answers `404 item_not_found`, and so does a `parentId` that names one. The project’s root item cannot be moved at all (`root_not_movable`). Any of those rejects the whole request and changes nothing. The batch is capped at 500 moves, and it is recorded as one step in the undo history.

This is the batch equivalent of `POST /v1/project/{projectId}/item/{itemId}/move`, and it is what the application’s own drag-and-drop calls when several nodes move at once.

itemId.description: ID of the item to move.

parentId.description: ID of the container to move it under, or `null` for the root, which is refused with `root_exists` when the project already has one. The project’s root item cannot be moved, so naming it rejects the whole batch with `root_not_movable`. Omit it to keep the current parent.

afterItemId.description: ID of the sibling to place it after. Omit it to append.

items.description: The moves to make, at most 500. They are applied in order, all of them or none: a single invalid id, parent or cycle rolls the batch back. An item may appear once, and no move may target another item in the same batch.

parameters.description: Project id: the value returned by the create endpoints, and the `id` of each row from `GET /v1/project`.

itemIds.description: IDs the request named, in the order they were given.

totalItems.description: Published item count the project reports after the write, as `GET /v1/project/{projectId}` returns it. Deleting or restoring items changes it; moving them does not.

post.description:
Copies an item and, by default, its direct children. The copy carries the item’s title, URL and type, its metadata, priority, change frequency, category, workflow status and colors — and its tags and content. Language alternates, the thumbnail and the link path are **not** copied, which is the application’s own rule: a copy is a new page that has not been given an address yet.

Omit `parentId` to copy the item where it stands, immediately after itself; send a container id to put the copy under it, or `null` for the root. A copy at the root is refused with `root_exists` on a project that already has one, so copying the root itself does not answer a second one. Only one level of children is copied — the children’s own children stay behind — so a copy of a deep container is a copy of its first level.

An item that has been deleted cannot be copied, and neither can a copy be put under a `parentId` that names one: both answer `404 item_not_found`.

Every copied item is published, and the set of new ids is recorded as one `copyItems` step in the undo history, so a single undo removes the whole copy.

parentId.description: ID of the container to put the copy under, or `null` for the root — refused with `root_exists` when the project already has a root, and copying the root itself would make a second one. Omit it to copy the item where it stands, immediately after it.

includeChildren.description: Whether to copy the item’s direct children as well, each with its own tags and content. Defaults to true. Only one level is copied, so the children’s children stay behind.
