post.summary: Sort the children of a container
post.description:
Reorders the published children of one container, or of the root. `itemIds` names the children to reorder and `parentId` the container they belong to; an id that is not a child of that container is ignored rather than rejected.

The children are ordered **by title**, not by the order of `itemIds`. Which comparison that means depends on the call, because it is the editor’s own behavior rather than a choice made here: naming `itemIds` compares those titles byte by byte, so uppercase sorts before lowercase and `Page 10` before `Page 2`; omitting them sorts every child naturally, with digit runs compared as numbers, so `Page 2` before `Page 10`. Both are reproduced so that sorting from this API and sorting from the editor leave the project in the same state — the two paths really do differ. If you need an order that is neither, move the items one at a time with `POST /v1/project/{projectId}/item/{itemId}/move` and `afterItemId`.

Omit `itemIds`, or send an empty array, to sort every child of the container by title. The sort is recorded as one step in the undo history, and the response lists the children in the order they were left in.

parentId.description: Container whose children to reorder. Omit it, or send `null`, to reorder the root items.

itemIds.description: Children to reorder, at most 500, each of them a child of `parentId` — an id that is not is ignored. The array names *which* children move, not the order they end up in — the application sorts the named children by title, and that behavior is reproduced here. Send an empty array, or omit it, to sort every child of the parent by title instead.

itemIds.description: Children of `parentId` after the sort, in the order they were left in.

post.description:
Reverses the newest edit in the project’s history — **whoever made it**. The stack is shared with the application, so an edit made in the editor can be undone here, and an edit made here can be undone in the editor. That is the point of sharing it, and it is also the reason to call it deliberately: you may be reversing someone else’s work, not just your own.

Everything the twelve kinds of edit can change is restored: an added item is deleted, a deleted subtree is republished, a rename is put back, a move returns to its previous parent and position, a sort returns to its previous order, and category, workflow status, tag and color edits are reverted to the values the item had. An undo does not undo the undo — it moves the history cursor back, so a following redo replays what was just reversed.

Nothing to undo answers `409` with `nothing_to_undo`, and nothing is changed. The response names the step that was reversed, which is the useful thing to log: the operation you called and the edit you affected are not always the same.

get.summary: List the content blocks of an item
get.description:
Returns every content block of one page, in the order the page renders them, each with the markup the application builds from it.

A block is one of six kinds — rich text, plain text, link, image, file and video — and each type reads different keys from `properties`. `rendered` is built from the stored values on every read rather than stored alongside them, so it always reflects the current renderer. The blocks are the editor’s material: they are what the content tab of an item shows, and a page with none is a page with no content.

The write that replaces this set is `PUT /v1/project/{projectId}/item/{itemId}/content`.

parameters.name: projectId
parameters.description: ID of the project the item belongs to.

parameters.name: itemId
parameters.description: ID of the item whose content blocks are read or replaced.

200.description: The item’s blocks in the order the page shows them, each with the markup the application renders.

id.description: ID of the block, unique within the item. It is what a write refers to: a block sent with this id is rewritten in place, a block sent without one is added, and a stored block the write leaves out is deleted.

type.description: Kind of block: `richtext`, `text`, `link`, `image`, `file` or `video`. It decides what `content` and `properties` mean and how the block renders, and it cannot be changed after the block is created.

content.description: The body the block renders. For `richtext` this is HTML as the page shows it, for `text` plain text that is escaped when rendered, and for a `video` whose `properties.custom` is set it is the embed markup. The application ignores it for `link`, `image` and `file` and renders those from `properties` alone.

properties.description:
Settings the block’s type reads, as an object of free-form keys, by type:

- `richtext`, `text` — no keys. The block renders `content` alone.
- `link` — `url` (required), `text` (the label; `#empty` is rendered when it is missing) and `newTab` (`1` to open the link in a new tab).
- `image` — `imageUrl` (the picture) for an image that links nowhere, or `custom: 1` with `url` (where the picture links to) and `alt` (its alternative text) for one that does.
- `file` — `url` (required, the file itself) and `name` (the label; `#empty` is rendered when it is missing).
- `video` — `url` (required) for a YouTube, Vimeo or Dailymotion page, or a `.mp4`/`.ogg` file, and `text` (the caption below the player); with `custom: 1` the block renders `content` instead and reads neither.

A key a type does not read is kept as stored and has no effect on the markup. The application writes the numeric keys as `0` and `1`, not as JSON booleans.

wrapper.description: Tag the application wraps the block in — `div`, `section`, `figure` and the other container tags this API accepts — or `none` for no wrapper at all. A block stored with no wrapper, an empty one, or one this API cannot safely interpolate into markup renders as `none`.

wrapperClass.description: Class the wrapper element carries. Empty when the wrapper has none.

wrapperId.description: ID the wrapper element carries. Empty when the wrapper has none.

settings.description: How the block is wrapped when it is rendered.

ordering.description: Position among the item’s blocks. A write sets it from the position of the block in the array it sends, so the array’s order is the page’s order, and the positions run from 1 without gaps afterwards. A page the application wrote may have blocks that share a position; a read returns those in id order.

rendered.description: The block as the application renders it into the page, wrapper included — an anchor for a `link`, an `img` for an `image`, a player embed for a `video`, the stored HTML for `richtext`. It is built from the stored values on every read, and its HTML is sanitized: scripts, event handlers and `javascript:` addresses are removed, while frames, media and inline SVG survive. A `<form>` and its controls are removed and their text kept, so a page that pasted one renders without it.

items.description: The blocks of the item, in render order.

put.summary: Replace the content blocks of an item
put.description:
Replaces every content block of one page with the blocks in the request, in the order they are sent. It is the only write: the editor holds the whole set, so a partial update would have to invent what it means for the blocks it was not told about.

The set is the unit, and the array position is the page’s order. A block sent with an `id` is rewritten in place — its content, properties, settings and position are replaced, and its `type` must be the one it was created with. A block sent without an id is added and answered with the id it was given. A stored block that is absent from the array is deleted, together with the link the application keeps between that block and the template it came from; an empty array therefore clears the page without touching the item.

The whole request is checked before anything is written, and a single bad block refuses all of them, so a caller never ends up with half the page it sent. HTML sent as `richtext`, or as the content of a custom `video` embed, is sanitized on the way in, and again when `rendered` is built. The response is the set as stored, in the same shape the read returns, including the ids new blocks were given.

id.description: ID of a block this item already holds, as a read returned it. The block is rewritten in place with this content, these settings and this position. Leave it out — or send `null` or `0` — to add a new block.

type.description: Kind of the block. One of the six the application renders; a block created with one type cannot become another, so a block that needs a different type has to be deleted and added.

content.description: Body of the block, interpreted as the read describes it. HTML sent for a `richtext` block, or for a custom `video` embed, is sanitized before it is stored. Omitted means empty. The ceilings are 1 MB for `richtext`, 256 KB for `text` and 64 KB for the other four.

properties.description:
The keys the block’s type reads, by type:

- `richtext`, `text` — no keys. The block renders `content` alone.
- `link` — `url` (required), `text` (the label; `#empty` is rendered when it is missing) and `newTab` (`1` to open the link in a new tab).
- `image` — `imageUrl` (the picture) for an image that links nowhere, or `custom: 1` with `url` (where the picture links to) and `alt` (its alternative text) for one that does.
- `file` — `url` (required, the file itself) and `name` (the label; `#empty` is rendered when it is missing).
- `video` — `url` (required) for a YouTube, Vimeo or Dailymotion page, or a `.mp4`/`.ogg` file, and `text` (the caption below the player); with `custom: 1` the block renders `content` instead and reads neither.

A key a type does not read is kept as stored and has no effect on the markup. The application writes the numeric keys as `0` and `1`, not as JSON booleans.

An address that reaches an `href` or a `src` must be absolute `http(s)`; a protocol-relative `//` address is accepted too, and a `link` may be a `mailto:` address. A block the application stored with a relative address is refused for the same reason, so a page that holds one has to have that block corrected or left out of the write. Omitted means no keys, which leaves a `link`, `image`, `file` or non-custom `video` with nothing to render. The object may hold up to 64 KB.

settings.description: How the block is wrapped when it is rendered. Omitted means no wrapper. The object may hold up to 64 KB.

wrapper.description: Container tag to wrap the block in, for example `div`, `section` or `figure`. Omitted or empty means `none`, which renders the block’s markup on its own. Only container tags are accepted: anything else is refused rather than stored.

wrapperClass.description: Class for the wrapper element. Omitted means empty; ignored when there is no wrapper.

wrapperId.description: ID for the wrapper element. Omitted means empty; ignored when there is no wrapper.

items.description: Every block the item should end up with, in the order the page should show them. The set is replaced wholesale: a block whose id is sent is rewritten, a block without an id is added, and a stored block that is not in the array is deleted. Send an empty array to remove every block. At most 500 blocks, and 5 MB across the request.

413.description: The request carries more than the call stores, and nothing was changed: `code` is `payload_too_large`. The ceilings are 500 blocks per item, 1 MB of `content` in a `richtext` block, 256 KB in a `text` block, 64 KB in any other block’s `content`, 64 KB each for `properties` and `settings`, and 5 MB across the request. A body over 6 MB is refused by the server before the handler runs, with `code` `FST_ERR_CTP_BODY_TOO_LARGE`. post.summary: Create a project from a URL
post.description:
Starts a crawl of a website and creates a project from it. The call returns as soon as the crawl is queued: the response carries the new project id and the login prompts the crawl may ask for. Progress is reported by `GET /v1/project/url/{id}`, and a crawl that has not started yet can be canceled with `DELETE /v1/project/url/{id}`.

The body is the crawl’s configuration. Without `maxPages` the account’s page allowance is used, and a larger value is lowered to it. `authOptions.id` names a saved login definition from `GET /v1/project/custom-login` and `authOptions.inputs` supplies its values in the order that listing returns them. A crawl that signs in can stop and ask for more while it runs: the `loginInputs` in this response are the prompts it may use, each answered through `PUT /v1/project/{projectId}/login-inputs/{inputId}`. `skipLinks`, `includeLinks` and `excludeLinks` match against the full URL of each link, and `includeLinksByProject` narrows the crawl to chosen items of a project that already exists.

The submitted URL is followed through up to five redirects before the crawl starts, so the project is created for the address it finally lands on. It must be reachable from the API: an address that cannot be fetched, or that redirects more than five times, answers 500 before any project is written. The project counts against the plan’s project allowance; at the allowance the call answers 500 “You have reached your project limit”. For a private SharePoint team site use `POST /v1/project/sharepoint`, and for a text list of URLs or an XML sitemap use `POST /v1/project/text` or `POST /v1/project/xml`. Read the project itself through `GET /v1/project/{projectId}` once the crawl finishes.

url.title: URL
url.description: URL the crawl starts from. The scheme must be `http` or `https`.

followRobots.title: Follow robots.txt
followRobots.description: When `true`, the crawler obeys the site's `robots.txt` and skips every page it disallows. Defaults to `true`.

followSubdomains.title: Follow subdomains
followSubdomains.description: When `true`, the crawler also visits subdomains of the start URL, such as `blog.example.com`. Defaults to `false`.

ignoreTrailingSlash.title: Ignore trailing slash
ignoreTrailingSlash.description: When `true`, `/about` and `/about/` count as one page, so the second one crawled is dropped. Defaults to `true`.

ignoreQueryString.title: Ignore query string
ignoreQueryString.description: When `true`, URLs that differ only in their query string count as one page, so the second one crawled is dropped. Defaults to `false`.

includeRedirects.title: Include redirects
includeRedirects.description: When `true`, a URL that redirects is kept in the sitemap next to its destination. Defaults to `false`.

includeBadLinks.title: Include bad links
includeBadLinks.description: When `true`, pages that answered `4xx` or `5xx` are kept in the sitemap instead of dropped. Defaults to `false`.

renderJavascript.title: Render JavaScript
renderJavascript.description: When `true`, pages are rendered in a headless browser before they are read, so links and content that JavaScript adds are found. Defaults to `false`.

includeContent.title: Include content
includeContent.description: When `true`, each page's body is stored with its item; the XPath fields narrow which part. Defaults to `false`.

uniquePageTitle.title: Unique page title
uniquePageTitle.description: When `true`, a page whose title matches one already crawled is dropped as a duplicate. Defaults to `false`.

ignoreScheme.title: Ignore scheme
ignoreScheme.description: When `true`, `http://` and `https://` versions of a URL count as one page. Defaults to `true`.

arrangeLinksByUrl.title: Arrange links by URL
arrangeLinksByUrl.description: When `true`, the tree follows each URL's path, so `/a/b` nests under `/a` even when the crawl found it elsewhere. Defaults to `true`.

domainAsRoot.title: Domain as root
domainAsRoot.description: When `true`, the tree is rooted at the domain rather than at the start URL, which matters when the start URL is a subdomain or subdirectory. Defaults to `false`.

includePdf.title: Include PDF
includePdf.description: When `true`, links to PDF files are kept in the sitemap. Defaults to `false`.

startUrlAsRoot.title: Start URL as root
startUrlAsRoot.description: When `true`, the tree is rooted at the start URL rather than at the domain. It has no effect unless `arrangeLinksByUrl` is also `true`. Defaults to `false`.

get.description:
Get the status and progress of a project that is being crawled.

Pass the project id returned by `POST /v1/project/url` or `POST /v1/project/sharepoint`: both submit a crawl and answer a project id, and the call reports either. Poll it as soon as the create call returns — the project exists while the crawl is still queued.

`status` goes from `PENDING` (queued) to `RUNNING` (pages being crawled) to `PERSIST` (results being written into the project) and finally `FINISHED` (the crawl is complete and the project is ready to read). `data` is `null` until the crawler reports progress, then carries `pageCount`, `downloadCount` and `crawlTime` in milliseconds; poll again for newer figures.

A SharePoint crawl has to sign in to the team site, so it can stop and wait for a Microsoft prompt — an MFA code, for example. The job stays `RUNNING` while it waits; the prompts are listed by `GET /v1/project/{projectId}/login-inputs` and answered with `PUT /v1/project/{projectId}/login-inputs/{inputId}`.

Projects imported from a text or XML file are not crawled this way: their progress comes from `GET /v1/project/text/{id}` and `GET /v1/project/xml/{id}`. A finished job is only readable while the crawler keeps it; once it is discarded the request answers an error, and the project itself is read through `GET /v1/project/{projectId}`. Because the job is read from the crawler rather than from the database, a project this API did not create from a URL, a project with no crawl job, and a discarded job all answer 500 with the reason instead of 404.

delete.description:
Cancels a crawl that has not started yet and deletes the project it was creating. Only a project in the pending state can be canceled: once the crawl is running, or once the project is published, this answers 500 “Project is not in cancellable state”. It is also the only way this API deletes a URL project — there is no delete endpoint for one that has already been crawled.

After it succeeds the project id stops resolving at `GET /v1/project/{projectId}`, and `GET /v1/project/url/{id}` answers 500 because the project is deleted. An id that does not exist, or that belongs to another account, answers 500 rather than 404. To stop a re-crawl of a published project use `DELETE /v1/project/url/{id}/refresh` instead.

post.description:
Re-crawls a project that was created from a URL and merges the results into it, instead of creating a second project. The project must already be published: a crawl that is still pending answers 500 “Project does not exist”, because only a finished crawl can be refreshed. Choose what the re-crawl may change with `addNewPages`, `updateTitles`, `overwriteMetadata` and `overwriteContent`; omitting them means none of those changes are applied.

A project that signs in to its website needs `authOptions.inputs` on every refresh. The credentials were never stored, so the login has to be repeated, and a refresh without them answers 400 `login_inputs_required` before anything is written. When the login is accepted the response also carries `loginInputs`: the prompts the re-crawl may stop on, answered with `PUT /v1/project/{projectId}/login-inputs/{inputId}` exactly as for the first crawl.

The re-crawl is queued and this call returns immediately. Nothing reports its progress: `GET /v1/project/url/{id}` keeps reporting the original crawl job, and the refresh only becomes visible as changed content at `GET /v1/project/{projectId}`. Cancel an outstanding refresh with `DELETE /v1/project/url/{id}/refresh`.

speed.title: Speed
speed.description: Pace of the re-crawl. `slower` throttles it, `slowest` throttles it further; omit it to crawl as fast as the crawler allows.

overwriteMetadata.title: Overwrite metadata
overwriteMetadata.description: Replace the metadata already stored on the project’s items with what the re-crawl finds. Defaults to false, which leaves existing metadata alone.

addNewPages.title: Add new pages
addNewPages.description: Add pages the re-crawl finds that the project does not have yet. Defaults to false, so a refresh with every option off only re-reads the pages that are already there.

updateTitles.title: Update titles
updateTitles.description: Replace existing item titles with the titles the re-crawl finds. Defaults to false.

overwriteContent.title: Overwrite content
overwriteContent.description: Replace existing page content with what the re-crawl downloads. Defaults to false.

delete.description:
Cancels every queued or running refresh of a project and leaves the project and its pages as they are. Unlike the import refresh cancels, this call is not idempotent: a project with nothing outstanding answers 500 “No outstanding refresh found for project ID {id}”, so treat that message as “nothing to cancel” rather than retrying. Refreshes are looked up within this account, so an id that does not exist and one that belongs to another account answer the same way.

A refresh is started with `POST /v1/project/url/{id}/refresh` and is not reported anywhere while it runs — see that endpoint. Canceling the original crawl is a different call, `DELETE /v1/project/url/{id}`, and only works before the crawl starts.

post.description:
Creates a project that was never imported from anywhere: no crawl, no file, no address to fetch. The application offers the same thing as its “Create from Scratch” action.

The project is published at once and is editable immediately, so this is the creation call for a sitemap that is going to be built by hand through the item endpoints. It starts with one page, a root item titled `Home` at `https://www.example.com`, which is also the project’s domain and its placeholder image. That address is a placeholder rather than a page that was fetched: nothing is crawled and nothing is fetched, so the root is free to be renamed and re-addressed by the first edit. The whole body is optional — send nothing and the project is called `Untitled Project`.

The project counts against the plan’s project allowance, and at the allowance the call answers 400 `project_limit_reached`. For a project that is populated from outside use `POST /v1/project/url`, `POST /v1/project/text`, `POST /v1/project/xml` or `POST /v1/project/sharepoint`; those answer a job status of their own, while this one is complete when it returns. Read the project with `GET /v1/project/{projectId}` and its tree with `GET /v1/project/{projectId}/item`.

get.summary: Get text import status and progress
get.description:
Reports the import started by `POST /v1/project/text`, one row for the run: whether it has finished, when it started and finished, how many of the URLs in the file have been read, and the last URL it processed.

Poll this after the create call until `finished` is true. The project it belongs to is readable meanwhile through `GET /v1/project/{projectId}`, while it is still pending. The task is looked up through the project’s text import record, so an id that is not a text-import project, a deleted one, or one belonging to another account answers 500 with the reason rather than 404.

A refresh started by `POST /v1/project/text/{id}/refresh` reports here too, because the project’s import record is pointed at the new task. Cancel the import with `DELETE /v1/project/text/{id}`, or just its outstanding refresh with `DELETE /v1/project/text/{id}/refresh`.

Cancels the import and deletes the project it created. The import service is told to stop, and the project is marked deleted in the same breath, so the project id stops resolving at `GET /v1/project/{projectId}` and this status endpoint answers 500 afterwards.

Only a text-import project can be canceled this way. An already-published project is deleted too — this is not limited to the pending state the way `DELETE /v1/project/url/{id}` is. If the import service cannot be reached the project is still marked deleted and the call answers 500, so a retry then reports that it has already been deleted.

post.summary: Refresh a project from its text file
post.description:
Re-imports a text project from the URL it was created from, instead of creating a second project. The project must be published, and it must have been created from a `url`: a project created from an uploaded file or a `fileKey` keeps no source URL, so it answers 500 “Project created from file upload can not be refreshed”. `GET /v1/project/{projectId}` reports the same fact as `allowTextRefresh`.

One refresh at a time: while a refresh of this project is queued or running, another answers 500 and asks you to wait, so cancel the outstanding one first if you need to change the options. `addNewPages` and `updateTitles` decide what the re-import may change; omitting them changes neither.

get.summary: Get XML import status and progress
get.description:
Reports the import started by `POST /v1/project/xml`, one row for the run: whether it has finished, when it started and finished, how many of the URLs in the sitemap have been read, and the last URL it processed.

Poll this after the create call until `finished` is true. The project it belongs to is readable meanwhile through `GET /v1/project/{projectId}`, while it is still pending. The task is looked up through the project’s XML import record, so an id that is not an XML-import project, a deleted one, or one belonging to another account answers 500 with the reason rather than 404.

A refresh started by `POST /v1/project/xml/{id}/refresh` reports here too, because the project’s import record is pointed at the new task. Cancel the import with `DELETE /v1/project/xml/{id}`, or just its outstanding refresh with `DELETE /v1/project/xml/{id}/refresh`.

post.description:
Create a project from a private SharePoint team site.

The crawl runs with a fixed scope: platform plumbing and first-party Microsoft domains are excluded, and the sign-in goes through the Microsoft login form with the supplied credentials. Nothing else about the crawl is configurable — the scope, the depth and the login recipe are set by the platform, unlike a generic crawl started with `POST /v1/project/url`.

The crawl is reported by `GET /v1/project/url/{id}`, which answers its status and progress while it runs. When the account is protected by MFA the crawl pauses. Poll `GET /v1/project/{projectId}/login-inputs` for the prompt and submit the code with `PUT /v1/project/{projectId}/login-inputs/{inputId}`. The prompts the crawl may use are already listed in this response, so their ids are known before the pause happens.

The project is stored private and flagged as a SharePoint project, which is also what makes it eligible for DACQ rather than VACQ — see `GET /v1/project/{projectId}/dacq`. The credentials are forwarded to the crawler and never stored. The project counts against the plan’s project allowance, and at the allowance the call answers 400 `project_limit_reached`.

password.description: Password of that account. It is sent to the crawler and never stored. If the account requires MFA, the project reports login inputs to answer during the crawl.

Position of the input in this list, used as `inputId` when submitting its value.

description.description: What the prompt asks for, in the words of the login recipe. An empty string when it carries no explanation.

get.summary: List login inputs a crawl is waiting for
get.description:
Get the login inputs a running crawl is waiting for.

A crawl that has to sign in through a multi-step login can stop and ask the user for a value — an MFA code, for example. Each input keeps its position for the lifetime of the crawl, and an input that has expired is reported as completed rather than disappearing, so an id never comes to mean a different prompt.

Returns an empty list for projects that cannot have login inputs. The project may still be pending: that is exactly when a crawl asks for input. Poll this while `GET /v1/project/url/{id}` reports the crawl as `RUNNING`, and answer the prompt with `PUT /v1/project/{projectId}/login-inputs/{inputId}`.

parameters.name: projectId
parameters.description: ID of the project whose crawl to inspect, as returned by POST /v1/project/url or POST /v1/project/sharepoint.

200.description: Every login prompt of the project’s current crawl, in the order it will ask for them.

id.description: Position of the input, 0-based. Submit its value to this id; it never changes for the life of the crawl.

label.description: Short label of the prompt, for example `Microsoft Authenticator approval`. Defaults to `Input` when the login recipe gives none.

description.description: What the prompt asks for, in the words of the login recipe. An empty string when it carries no explanation.

ready.description: 1 once the crawl is actually waiting for this value, 0 before it reaches the prompt.

completed.description: 1 once the input has been answered or has expired, 0 while it is still outstanding. An expired input is reported completed rather than removed, so ids never come to mean a different prompt.

value.description: Value of the input: what the crawl filled in to show the user something (the number to match in an authenticator app, for example), or the value a client submitted. Empty when the crawl is waiting for a value and has none of its own.

items.description: Every login prompt of the project’s current crawl, in the order the crawl will ask for them.

put.description:
Submit the value of a login input, which releases the crawl to continue signing in.

Omit `value` — send an empty object — when the input already carries the value the crawl needs, such as a Microsoft Authenticator approval where the crawl reports the number to match and only waits to be told to continue. post.summary: Create a project from a text file
post.description:
Creates a project from a plain-text list of URLs, imported rather than crawled. Send one source: a `file` part (maximum 64 MB), a `fileKey` returned by `POST /v1/files` for a file uploaded with the `project_text` purpose, or a `url` the import service fetches. A request with none of the three answers 400 `invalid_file_source`, and so does a `fileKey` combined with either of the others; a `url` sent alongside a `file` takes precedence, and the file is not used.

A multipart request carries the options as a JSON `body` field next to the file; a JSON request carries `fileKey`, `speed` and `url` at the top level. The file type is checked against the purpose: text files, JSON, XML and YAML are accepted, and anything else answers 400 `invalid_file_type`. An empty file answers 400 `file_empty`, and one over 64 MB answers 413 `file_too_large`.

The import is queued. The response is only the new project id: poll `GET /v1/project/text/{id}` until `finished` is true, then read the project through `GET /v1/project/{projectId}`. Cancel it with `DELETE /v1/project/text/{id}`. A project created from a file or a `fileKey` cannot be refreshed, because no source URL is kept for it; if you will need `POST /v1/project/text/{id}/refresh`, create the project from a `url`. The project counts against the plan’s project allowance, and at the allowance the call answers 500 “You have reached your project limit”.

get.summary: List the links found by a crawl
get.description:
Lists what the project’s crawl found on the site: one row per distinct host and path, with the status the URL answered, the element it was found in, and how many references to it the crawl counted. This is the inventory a crawled project has, and the list to page through when you want to know which URLs are broken, unindexable or pointing off-site.

`{projectId}` is the project id returned by `GET /v1/project`, and also the id the project’s crawl is stored under. Rows are grouped by host and path, so variants of the same URL collapse into one row instead of appearing once per reference, and `occurrences` reports how many references the crawl counted for it. `total` counts the distinct URLs the filters matched, `limit` defaults to 100 and `page` to 1, and `pageSize` reports how many pages of that size the match spans, so you can stop at the first page whose number exceeds it.

`status` buckets the HTTP status the URL answered, `type` buckets it by media type, `location` separates links inside the site from links leaving it, and `discoverability` filters on what the crawler’s `robots` data allowed. `search` matches the URL and the recorded anchor text, `language` matches the page’s language code exactly, and `orderBy` defaults to link id.

Inventory exists only once a crawl has run: a project that has never been crawled, or whose crawl stored no job, answers 500 rather than an empty page, and a `{projectId}` that is not a number answers 500 rather than 400. For the totals alone use `GET /v1/inventory/{projectId}/summary`, for the links found on one page of the sitemap use `GET /v1/inventory/{projectId}/{itemId}`, and for where one of these rows is referenced use `GET /v1/inventory/{projectId}/{linkId}/occurrences` with `items[].id` as `linkId`.

parameters.name: limit
parameters.description: Maximum number of links to return in this page. Defaults to 100. A negative value is treated as 0, which returns no rows, and no upper bound is applied, so a large value returns a large page.

parameters.name: page
parameters.description: 1-based page number to return. Defaults to 1, and a value below 1 is treated as 1. A page past the end answers an empty `items` with the full `total` still reported.

parameters.name: orderBy
parameters.description: Field to sort by. `occurrence` puts the most referenced URLs first, `status` sorts ascending by HTTP status, `id` sorts ascending by link id and `last_modified` puts the most recently modified pages first. Defaults to `id`.

parameters.name: search
parameters.description: Text to match against the link’s URL and the anchor text recorded for it, compared with SQL `LIKE`, so `%` and `_` act as wildcards rather than literal characters. A numeric value also matches links whose stored status equals that number exactly.

parameters.name: status
parameters.description: HTTP status bucket to keep. `ok` is 200–299, `bad` is 400–599, `redirect` is 300–399 and `unexpected` is a stored status above 599 — a link the crawl got no HTTP response for, so a range no HTTP status can occupy. No value selects 100–199 or a link with no stored status, and omitting the parameter keeps every status.

parameters.name: type
parameters.description: Media type to keep, decided from the response MIME type and the URL’s file extension. `page` is HTML answered with a status between 200 and 599; `image` is a PNG, JPEG, GIF, WebP or SVG answered successfully; `document` is a PDF, Word, Excel or PowerPoint file; `audio` is MP3, WAV, OGG, AAC or FLAC; `video` is MP4, WebM, OGV, AVI, MOV or MKV, or an embedded YouTube, Dailymotion or Vimeo player; `file` is any other successful response that is not HTML, an image, a document, audio or video.

parameters.name: location
parameters.description: `internal` keeps links that stay on the crawled site and `external` keeps links that point at another site, matching the `isExternal` field of each row. Omitting the parameter keeps both.

parameters.name: language
parameters.description: Language code recorded for the page, such as `en`, matched exactly rather than as a prefix. A page whose language the crawl did not record never matches, so sending it narrows the result to pages with a known language.

parameters.name: discoverability
parameters.description: What the site’s `robots` data allowed for the link. `crawlable` and `non-crawlable` keep links whose directives allow, or forbid, following them; `indexable` and `non-indexable` do the same for indexing; `orphan` keeps links that no page in the site is recorded as linking to. Only one of the five can be sent, and omitting it keeps every link.

parameters.name: projectId
parameters.description: Project id: the value returned by the create endpoints, and the `id` of each row from `GET /v1/project`.

200.description: A page of the links the project’s crawl recorded.

total.description: Number of distinct URLs the filters matched across every page, not the number in this page.

limit.description: Page size this response was built with: `limit` from the query, or 100 when it was omitted. Negative values arrive as 0.

page.description: 1-based page this response holds: `page` from the query, or 1 when it was omitted.

pageSize.description: Number of pages of `limit` rows the match spans — `ceil(total / limit)` — so the last page is this number and a larger `page` is past the end. 0 when `limit` is 0.

id.description: ID of the link. Pass it as `{linkId}` to `GET /v1/inventory/{projectId}/{linkId}/occurrences`.

sourceTag.description: Name of the HTML element the link was found in, such as `a`, `area`, `img`, `iframe`, `frame` or `link`. `null` when the crawler recorded the URL without an element, for example a URL it reached while following a redirect.

url.description: URL as the crawl recorded it. Empty string when the crawler stored none.

title.description: Title of the page at this URL. Empty string when the page declares no title or was never fetched.

status.description: HTTP status the URL answered: 200–299 for a success, 300–399 for a redirect, 400–599 for a client or server error, and a value above 599 for a link the crawl got no HTTP response for, which is the range the `unexpected` filter selects. 0 when no status was stored at all.

mimetype.description: MIME type the response declared, for example `text/html` for a page or `image/png` for an image. `null` when the crawl recorded none, which is usual for a URL that never answered.

encoding.description: Character encoding the crawl stored for the response body, for example `utf-8`. `null` when none was recorded.

isExternal.description: Whether the URL points at another site rather than the crawled one: `true` for a link that leaves the site, `false` for one inside it. This is the field the `location` filter matches.

occurrences.description: How many references to this URL the crawl counted. 0 when the crawler reached the URL without finding a reference to it in the site’s own markup.

linkText.description: Text the crawler captured along with the reference, which for a plain link is its anchor text. Empty string when nothing was captured.

metaDescription.description: Description meta tag of the page at this URL. Empty string when the page declares none.

metaKeywords.description: Keywords meta tag of the page at this URL. Empty string when the page declares none.

language.description: Language code the crawl recorded for the page, such as `en`. `null` when none was recorded, and the `language` query parameter matches this value exactly.

lastModified.description: Value of the page’s `Last-Modified` response header, stored as the server sent it and so not necessarily ISO 8601. `null` when the response carried no such header.

headers.description: Response headers captured for the page, one `[name, value]` pair per header: element 0 is the header name and element 1 its value. Ordered by header name. Empty when no headers were stored for the URL.

get.summary: Get the inventory summary of a project
get.description:
One call for the numbers behind the inventory: how many pages the crawl found, how many internal and external links it recorded, and how many of those links failed. Use it to size a project before paging through `GET /v1/inventory/{projectId}`, or to render a header without fetching a single row.

`{projectId}` is the project id returned by `GET /v1/project`, and also the id the project’s crawl is stored under. Every count comes from the statistics the crawl itself stored, so they measure what the crawler counted. The inventory list counts distinct URLs instead, so its `total` matches neither `internalLinks` nor `externalLinks`.

`badLinks` counts links that answered 400–599 and `errors` counts links stored with a status above 599 — a link the crawl got no HTTP response for — so the second range is one no HTTP status can occupy. The two ranges do not overlap, so a link is counted in at most one of them. `subdomains` lists the other hosts the crawl treated as part of the site, with `www.` stripped and the site’s own host removed.

A project that has never been crawled has no crawler record and answers 500 rather than zeroes or a 404, and a project whose stored crawl statistics cannot be read answers 500 for the same reason. Zeroes are a real answer only for a crawl that ran and found nothing. The inventory itself is listed by `GET /v1/inventory/{projectId}`.

parameters.name: projectId
parameters.description: Project id: the value returned by the create endpoints, and the `id` of each row from `GET /v1/project`.

200.description: The counts behind the project inventory.

subdomains.description: Other hosts the crawl treated as part of the site — the subdomains it found, such as `blog.example.com`, with `www.` stripped and the site’s own host removed. Empty when the crawl reported none.

pages.description: Number of pages the crawl found on the site.

internalLinks.description: Number of internal links the crawl recorded. Some crawls store no link counts at all, and this field is published as a number rather than a nullable one, so the endpoint answers 500 instead of returning `null` in that case.

externalLinks.description: Number of links pointing at other sites that the crawl recorded. Published as a number, so a crawl that stored no such count leaves the endpoint answering 500 rather than `null`.

badLinks.description: Links that answered 400–599, summed from the crawl’s stored status counts.

errors.description: Links stored with a status above 599 — a link the crawl got no HTTP response for. Disjoint from `badLinks`, which counts 400–599 only.

get.summary: List the links on a sitemap item
get.description:
Lists the links the crawl found on one page of the project’s sitemap: every URL referenced from the page behind that sitemap item, with the same columns the project inventory returns minus the response headers. Use it to answer what a single page links to, and which of those links are broken, without paging the whole inventory.

`{projectId}` is the project id returned by `GET /v1/project`. `{itemId}` is a sitemap item id — the `id` of an item from `GET /v1/project/{projectId}/item` or `GET /v1/project/{projectId}/item/{itemId}`, never a link id. The item is first resolved to the page the last crawl found for it, so an item that maps to no crawled page — a sitemap `container`, which is a bucket rather than a page, or an item the crawl never reached — answers 500 because that lookup returns nothing. An `{itemId}` that is not a number also answers 500 rather than 400.

Paging and filtering work as in `GET /v1/inventory/{projectId}`: `total` counts the links that matched, `limit` defaults to 100, `page` defaults to 1, `pageSize` is the number of pages, and `orderBy` defaults to link id. `status`, `type`, `location`, `language` and `search` select and order rows the same way; the call has no `discoverability` filter.

A project that has never been crawled answers 500 rather than an empty list. Each row’s `id` is a link id, so it can be passed as `{linkId}` to `GET /v1/inventory/{projectId}/{linkId}/occurrences`.

parameters.name: limit
parameters.description: Maximum number of links to return in this page. Defaults to 100. A negative value is treated as 0, which returns no rows, and no upper bound is applied.

parameters.name: page
parameters.description: 1-based page number to return. Defaults to 1, and a value below 1 is treated as 1.

parameters.name: orderBy
parameters.description: Field to sort by. `occurrence` puts the links referenced most often first, `status` sorts ascending by HTTP status, `id` sorts ascending by link id and `last_modified` puts the most recently modified pages first. Defaults to `id`.

parameters.name: search
parameters.description: Text to match against the link’s URL and the anchor text this page used for it, compared with SQL `LIKE`, so `%` and `_` act as wildcards rather than literal characters. A numeric value also matches links whose stored status equals that number exactly.

parameters.name: status
parameters.description: HTTP status bucket to keep. `ok` is 200–299, `bad` is 400–599, `redirect` is 300–399 and `unexpected` is a stored status above 599 — a link the crawl got no HTTP response for, so a range no HTTP status can occupy. No value selects 100–199 or a link with no stored status.

parameters.name: type
parameters.description: Media type to keep, decided from the response MIME type and the URL’s file extension. `page` is HTML answered with a status between 200 and 599; `image` is a PNG, JPEG, GIF, WebP or SVG answered successfully; `document` is a PDF, Word, Excel or PowerPoint file; `audio` is MP3, WAV, OGG, AAC or FLAC; `video` is MP4, WebM, OGV, AVI, MOV or MKV, or an embedded YouTube, Dailymotion or Vimeo player; `file` is any other successful response that is not HTML, an image, a document, audio or video.

parameters.name: location
parameters.description: `internal` keeps links that stay on the crawled site and `external` keeps links that point at another site, matching the `isExternal` field of each row. Omitting the parameter keeps both.

parameters.name: language
parameters.description: Language code recorded for the page, such as `en`, matched exactly rather than as a prefix. A page whose language the crawl did not record never matches.

parameters.name: projectId
parameters.description: Project id: the value returned by the create endpoints, and the `id` of each row from `GET /v1/project`.

parameters.name: itemId
parameters.description: ID of a sitemap item, as returned by `GET /v1/project/{projectId}/item`.

200.description: A page of the links found on one sitemap item.

total.description: Number of links that matched across every page, not the number in this page.

limit.description: Page size this response was built with: `limit` from the query, or 100 when it was omitted. Negative values arrive as 0.

page.description: 1-based page this response holds: `page` from the query, or 1 when it was omitted.

pageSize.description: Number of pages of `limit` rows the match spans — `ceil(total / limit)` — so a larger `page` is past the end. 0 when `limit` is 0.

id.description: ID of the link found on this page. Pass it as `{linkId}` to `GET /v1/inventory/{projectId}/{linkId}/occurrences`.

sourceTag.description: Name of the HTML element the link was found in, such as `a`, `area`, `img`, `iframe`, `frame` or `link`. `null` when the crawler recorded the URL without an element.

url.description: URL of the linked resource as the crawl recorded it. Empty string when the crawler stored none.

title.description: Title of the page at this URL. Empty string when that page declares no title or was never fetched.

status.description: HTTP status the linked URL answered: 200–299 for a success, 300–399 for a redirect, 400–599 for a client or server error, and a value above 599 for a link the crawl got no HTTP response for, which is the range the `unexpected` filter selects. 0 when no status was stored at all.

mimetype.description: MIME type the response declared, for example `text/html` for a page or `image/png` for an image. `null` when the crawl recorded none, which is usual for a URL that never answered.

encoding.description: Character encoding the crawl stored for the response body, for example `utf-8`. `null` when none was recorded.

isExternal.description: Whether the URL points at another site rather than the crawled one: `true` for a link that leaves the site, `false` for one inside it. This is the field the `location` filter matches.

occurrences.description: How many references to this URL the crawl counted across the whole site, not only on the page being listed.

linkText.description: Anchor text this page used for the link. Empty string when nothing was captured.

metaDescription.description: Description meta tag of the page at this URL. Empty string when that page declares none.

metaKeywords.description: Keywords meta tag of the page at this URL. Empty string when that page declares none.

language.description: Language code the crawl recorded for the page at this URL, such as `en`. `null` when none was recorded, and the `language` query parameter matches this value exactly.

lastModified.description: Value of that page’s `Last-Modified` response header, stored as the server sent it and so not necessarily ISO 8601. `null` when the response carried no such header.

items.description: The links found on this sitemap item’s page, in the order requested by `orderBy`.

get.summary: List the pages that reference a link
get.description:
Lists where one link is used: each row is a page on the crawled site that contains a reference to the URL you asked about, with that page’s title and status and the anchor text it used. The same URL referenced from ten pages is one row in `GET /v1/inventory/{projectId}` and ten rows here, which is the call to make when you know a URL is broken or duplicated and want to find the pages that carry it.

`{projectId}` is the project id returned by `GET /v1/project`. `{linkId}` is a link id — `items[].id` from `GET /v1/inventory/{projectId}` or from `GET /v1/inventory/{projectId}/{itemId}`, never a sitemap item id. An id that no page references is not an error: `total` is 0 and `items` is empty. A `{linkId}` that is not a number answers 500 rather than 400.

Each returned `id` is the id of the referencing page, not of the link you asked about, so it can be paged like any other inventory row. `search` matches the anchor text, the page title and the page URL, `limit` defaults to 100 and `page` to 1, and `pageSize` reports how many pages the match spans.

A project that has never been crawled answers 500 rather than an empty list, because its inventory does not exist yet.

parameters.description: Maximum number of referencing pages to return in this page. Defaults to 100. A negative value is treated as 0, which returns no rows, and no upper bound is applied.

parameters.name: page
parameters.description: 1-based page number to return. Defaults to 1, and a value below 1 is treated as 1.

parameters.name: search
parameters.description: Text to match against the anchor text this page used, the page title and the page URL, compared with SQL `LIKE`, so `%` and `_` act as wildcards rather than literal characters.

parameters.name: projectId
parameters.description: Project id: the value returned by the create endpoints, and the `id` of each row from `GET /v1/project`.

parameters.name: linkId
parameters.description: ID of an inventory link, as returned in `items[].id` by `GET /v1/inventory/{projectId}` — not the id of a sitemap item.

total.description: Number of pages that reference the link across every page, not the number in this page.

limit.description: Page size this response was built with: `limit` from the query, or 100 when it was omitted. Negative values arrive as 0.

page.description: 1-based page this response holds: `page` from the query, or 1 when it was omitted.

pageSize.description: Number of pages of `limit` rows the match spans — `ceil(total / limit)` — so a larger `page` is past the end. 0 when `limit` is 0.

id.description: ID of the page that references the link — an inventory link id of its own, not the id you asked about.

url.description: URL of the referencing page. Empty string when the crawl stored none.

title.description: Title of the referencing page. Empty string when it declares none or was never fetched.

get.description:
Lists the audits this project has run, newest first: one row per run, with the issue counts that run recorded. This is the audit history, not the current state — the eleven issue endpoints and `GET /v1/audit/{projectId}/score` read the latest run alone, so use the call to show progress between runs, or to find out when a count was taken.

Each count is what the run found minus what the account has archived since, so archiving an issue in the application lowers these figures as well as removing the row from the issue lists. A project that has never been audited answers an empty page — `total: 0`, `items: []` — rather than a 404, and audits themselves are started in the application, not through this API.

Every audit operation requires the Content Audit feature on the account: without it the call answers 403 `feature_disabled`. A project the account cannot see answers 404 `project_not_found`, and one it can see but has not been granted access to answers 403 `unauthorized_access`.

get.summary: Get a project's content audit score
get.description:
Returns the content audit score of a project, computed from its latest run and reported on a 0-100 scale.

A private SharePoint site is not publicly indexable, so `crawlability` and `indexability` are `null` for those projects: a crawl and index ratio says nothing about quality where no search engine index exists. `score` is unaffected, because it measures duplicated and orphaned content rather than search visibility.

Before the project’s first audit there is no latest run, and the endpoint answers zeros — `score` 0, `crawlability` and `indexability` 0, or `null` for a private SharePoint project — rather than failing, so it is safe to call for any project without checking first. `GET /v1/audit/{projectId}` lists the runs behind the figure, and the eleven issue endpoints break the same run down.

Every audit operation requires the Content Audit feature on the account: without it the call answers 403 `feature_disabled`. A project the account cannot see answers 404 `project_not_found`, and one it can see but has not been granted access to answers 403 `unauthorized_access`.

parameters.name: projectId
parameters.description: Project id: the value returned by the create endpoints, and the `id` of each row from `GET /v1/project`.

200.description: The content audit score of the latest run.

score.description: Content score for the latest run, 0-100. It starts from the share of crawled pages the run recorded no content issue for; when the run found orphan pages, the reported figure is 91% of that share plus 9% of the share of orphan pages that have been archived, rounded. A run with no orphan pages reports the page share alone.

crawlability.description: Share of the latest run’s URLs whose robots directives allow a crawl, as a percentage. Null for private SharePoint projects.

indexability.description: Share of the latest run’s URLs whose robots directives allow indexing, as a percentage. Null for private SharePoint projects.

get.description:
Lists the links the latest run could not reach: one row per failing URL, with the status the run recorded and how often the URL was linked. A link belongs here when that status is 400 or above — including the crawler’s own codes above 599, which record an attempt that never produced an HTTP response — and the run either recorded the element that referenced it, found at least one page linking to it, or recorded that code at least once.

Rows are grouped by host and path, so a URL appears once in the list and `occurrences` is the count recorded for it. A `search` term of three digits between 200 and 599 is matched as the status itself, so `?search=404` narrows the list to one status code.

Reads the latest run only: `GET /v1/audit/{projectId}` lists every run of the project, newest first, and `GET /v1/audit/{projectId}/score` summarizes the newest one. A page fixed since that run still appears here until the next audit replaces it. Until the project has been audited once there is no latest run, and the call answers 500 `Project is not audited.` instead of an empty list.

Every audit operation requires the Content Audit feature on the account: without it the call answers 403 `feature_disabled`. A project the account cannot see answers 404 `project_not_found`, and one it can see but has not been granted access to answers 403 `unauthorized_access`.

parameters.name: search
parameters.description: Term matched against the URL of the affected page. A term starting with `http` is matched as a URL prefix; any other term is matched anywhere in the URL. Case sensitivity follows the database column’s collation. Omitted returns every row.

parameters.name: archived
parameters.description: Which archived state to list, as a string: `1` for issues the account has archived in the application, `0` for issues it has not. Defaults to `0`, so archived issues stay hidden unless asked for. A string rather than a JSON boolean because query parameters are always text.

parameters.name: limit
parameters.description: Number of rows to return per page. Defaults to 20.

parameters.name: page
parameters.description: Page to return, 1-based. Defaults to 1.

parameters.name: projectId
parameters.description: Project id: the value returned by the create endpoints, and the `id` of each row from `GET /v1/project`.

200.description: A page of failing links, grouped by host and path.

total.description: Number of failing URLs matching the filters, across every page rather than just this one.

limit.description: Page size used: the `limit` sent, or 20 when none was sent.

pageSize.description: Number of pages of results, `ceil(total / limit)` — how many requests the full list takes, not how many rows this response holds.

id.description: ID of the record the run holds for this URL. Identify the row by `url` rather than by this id.

url.description: The failing URL, as the run recorded it.

status.description: Status the run recorded for the URL. 400 to 599 are HTTP responses; values above 599 are the crawler’s own codes for attempts that never produced one.

occurrences.description: How many times the run recorded this URL as a link. Zero means nothing on the site links to it and the crawler reached it another way.

items.description: The failing URLs on this page, grouped by host and path.

get.description:
Lists the links the latest run recorded as client errors: one row per URL answered with a status between 400 and 499, which means the request itself was wrong — a stale, forbidden or mistyped address — rather than the server failing. Rows are grouped by host and path, and `occurrences` counts how often the URL was linked.

get.description:
Lists the meta descriptions the latest run found on more than one page: one row per duplicated description, not per page. `links` is how many pages share it and `urls` lists their addresses; a description repeated across a template makes those pages compete for the same snippet. A page with no description is on `GET /v1/audit/{projectId}/missing-description`, and one whose description is too long on `GET /v1/audit/{projectId}/long-description`.

The run records the duplicate groups and the call paginates them. `search` narrows the groups to those with a matching page URL and filters `urls` to the matches, while `links` keeps counting the whole group.

Reads the latest run only: `GET /v1/audit/{projectId}` lists every run of the project, newest first, and `GET /v1/audit/{projectId}/score` summarizes the newest one. A page fixed since that run still appears here until the next audit replaces it. Until the project has been audited once there is no latest run, and the call answers 500 `Project is not audited.` instead of an empty list.

Every audit operation requires the Content Audit feature on the account: without it the call answers 403 `feature_disabled`. A project the account cannot see answers 404 `project_not_found`, and one it can see but has not been granted access to answers 403 `unauthorized_access`.

get.description:
Lists the pages the latest run was not allowed to crawl: one row per page whose robots directives kept the crawler out. `robotsAllowed` is the crawl decision the run recorded for the page, `robotsNofollow` whether the page also tells crawlers not to follow its links, and `status` the HTTP status the run recorded when it fetched the page.

Reads the latest run only: `GET /v1/audit/{projectId}` lists every run of the project, newest first, and `GET /v1/audit/{projectId}/score` summarizes the newest one. A page fixed since that run still appears here until the next audit replaces it. Until the project has been audited once there is no latest run, and the call answers 500 `Project is not audited.` instead of an empty list.

Every audit operation requires the Content Audit feature on the account: without it the call answers 403 `feature_disabled`. A project the account cannot see answers 404 `project_not_found`, and one it can see but has not been granted access to answers 403 `unauthorized_access`.

Reads the latest run only: `GET /v1/audit/{projectId}` lists every run of the project, newest first, and `GET /v1/audit/{projectId}/score` summarizes the newest one. Every audit operation requires the Content Audit feature on the account: without it the call answers 403 `feature_disabled`. A project the account cannot see answers 404 `project_not_found`, and one it can see but has not been granted access to answers 403 `unauthorized_access`.

get.summary: Get analytics totals for a project
get.description:
Traffic totals for a project over a date range, taken from the Google Analytics 4 properties linked to the project. This is the headline call: `GET /v1/analytics/{projectId}/daily` breaks the same metrics down by day, `GET /v1/analytics/{projectId}/traffic-source` by channel and `GET /v1/analytics/{projectId}/pages` by page.

Both dates are required calendar dates in `YYYY-MM-DD` form, with no default, and the range includes both ends. The figures are the ones already collected for those properties — the call does not query Google Analytics itself, so a day only has numbers once it has been collected.

With several properties linked their rows are added together, so a user or a session seen on two properties is counted twice and revenue adds figures that may not share a currency. `averageSessionDuration` and `sessionConversionRate` average Google Analytics’ own per-row values rather than being recomputed; `engagementRate` and `bounceRate` are computed here from the summed sessions. A property that is linked but has no traffic in the range answers zeroes, while a project with no linked property at all answers 500: two of the eleven figures are never assembled in that case and the response cannot be filled in.

parameters.name: startDate
parameters.description: First calendar day of the range, in `YYYY-MM-DD` form. Required, with no default. Inclusive: traffic recorded for this day is included.

parameters.name: endDate
parameters.description: Last calendar day of the range, in `YYYY-MM-DD` form. Required, with no default. Inclusive. An `endDate` earlier than `startDate` is not rejected; it matches no rows.

parameters.name: projectId
parameters.description: ID of the project whose analytics are read. `GET /v1/project` lists the projects the token can see and returns each one’s `id`.

200.description: Totals for the whole range, across every property linked to the project.

activeUsers.description: Distinct users Google Analytics counted as active: a user is active once they have an engaged session.

newUsers.description: Users Google Analytics saw for the first time in the range.

sessions.description: Sessions Google Analytics counted. A visit is one session however many pages it covers.

engagedSessions.description: Sessions Google Analytics classes as engaged: those lasting longer than 10 seconds, containing a conversion, or viewing two or more pages.

averageSessionDuration.description: Mean length of a session in seconds, averaged over the stored daily rows rather than weighted by the number of sessions.

conversions.description: Conversion events — events the property marks as conversions, key events in newer Google Analytics wording.

sessionConversionRate.description: Share of sessions in which a user converted, averaged over the stored daily rows rather than recomputed from the summed sessions.

eventCount.description: Events recorded, under every event name.

get.summary: Get daily analytics totals for a project
get.description:
One row of traffic figures per stored day for a project, taken from the Google Analytics 4 properties linked to the project and ordered oldest first. Use it to chart a trend; `GET /v1/analytics/{projectId}` returns the same metrics totalled over the whole range.

Both dates are required calendar dates in `YYYY-MM-DD` form, with no default, and the range includes both ends. Days without collected data are absent rather than zero-filled. The rows come back as stored, without merging, so a day with figures from more than one property appears more than once; add those rows up yourself if you need one figure per day.

parameters.name: startDate
parameters.description: First calendar day of the range, in `YYYY-MM-DD` form. Required, with no default. Inclusive: traffic recorded for this day is included.

parameters.name: endDate
parameters.description: Last calendar day of the range, in `YYYY-MM-DD` form. Required, with no default. Inclusive. An `endDate` earlier than `startDate` is not rejected; it matches no rows.

parameters.name: projectId
parameters.description: ID of the project whose analytics are read. `GET /v1/project` lists the projects the token can see and returns each one’s `id`.

200.description: One row per stored day, oldest first, over the requested range.

date.description: Calendar day the row covers, in `YYYY-MM-DD` form.

activeUsers.description: Distinct users Google Analytics counted as active: a user is active once they have an engaged session.

newUsers.description: Users Google Analytics saw for the first time on that day.

sessions.description: Sessions Google Analytics counted. A visit is one session however many pages it covers.

engagedSessions.description: Sessions Google Analytics classes as engaged: those lasting longer than 10 seconds, containing a conversion, or viewing two or more pages.

averageSessionDuration.description: Mean length of a session in seconds for that day, as Google Analytics recorded it.

conversions.description: Conversion events — events the property marks as conversions, key events in newer Google Analytics wording.

sessionConversionRate.description: Share of that day’s sessions in which a user converted, as Google Analytics recorded it.

eventCount.description: Events recorded, under every event name.

totalRevenue.description: Revenue from purchases, subscriptions and advertising, in the currency of each property. The currency code is not returned.

engagementRate.description: Engaged sessions divided by sessions, between 0 and 1, and 0 when there are no sessions. Computed by this API from the summed sessions rather than read from Google Analytics.

bounceRate.description: Sessions that were not engaged, divided by all sessions, between 0 and 1 — the exact complement of `engagementRate`, and computed by this API for the same reason.

data.description: The days of the range that have collected figures, oldest first.

get.description:
One row per Google Analytics default channel group — `Direct`, `Organic Search`, `Referral`, `Email` and the rest — with the traffic that channel produced over the range, largest by active users first. Channels are grouped across the properties linked to the project and across the days in the range, so each channel appears once.

Both dates are required calendar dates in `YYYY-MM-DD` form, with no default, and the range includes both ends. `averageSessionDuration` and `sessionConversionRate` here are Google Analytics’ stored daily values added together rather than averaged, so compare channels by them only loosely. A project with no linked property, or a range with no traffic, answers an empty `data` array.

parameters.name: startDate
parameters.description: First calendar day of the range, in `YYYY-MM-DD` form. Required, with no default. Inclusive: traffic recorded for this day is included.

parameters.name: endDate
parameters.description: Last calendar day of the range, in `YYYY-MM-DD` form. Required, with no default. Inclusive. An `endDate` earlier than `startDate` is not rejected; it matches no rows.

parameters.name: projectId
parameters.description: ID of the project whose analytics are read. `GET /v1/project` lists the projects the token can see and returns each one’s `id`.

200.description: One row per Google Analytics default channel group, largest by active users first.

sessionDefaultChannelGroup.description: Channel Google Analytics grouped the sessions into with its default channel grouping — `Direct`, `Organic Search`, `Paid Search`, `Organic Social`, `Paid Social`, `Referral`, `Email`, `Display`, `Affiliates` and the other channels in that grouping — or `Unassigned` when none of them applies.

activeUsers.description: Distinct users Google Analytics counted as active: a user is active once they have an engaged session.

sessions.description: Sessions Google Analytics counted. A visit is one session however many pages it covers.

engagedSessions.description: Sessions Google Analytics classes as engaged: those lasting longer than 10 seconds, containing a conversion, or viewing two or more pages.

averageSessionDuration.description: The stored daily averages added together, in seconds — a sum of averages, so not the channel’s true mean session length.

conversions.description: Conversion events — events the property marks as conversions, key events in newer Google Analytics wording.

sessionConversionRate.description: The stored daily rates added together across the days in the range rather than averaged, so not the channel’s true conversion rate.

eventCount.description: Events recorded, under every event name.

totalRevenue.description: Revenue from purchases, subscriptions and advertising, in the currency of each property. The currency code is not returned.

engagementRate.description: Engaged sessions divided by sessions, between 0 and 1, and 0 when there are no sessions. Computed by this API from the summed sessions rather than read from Google Analytics.

bounceRate.description: Sessions that were not engaged, divided by all sessions, between 0 and 1 — the exact complement of `engagementRate`, and computed by this API for the same reason.

data.description: One row per channel group that drove traffic in the range, largest by active users first.

get.summary: List events and their traffic metrics
get.description:
One row per event name recorded over the range, most frequent first: `page_view`, `session_start`, `purchase` and whatever else the properties linked to the project collected. Events are grouped by name across properties and days, so each name appears once.

Both dates are required calendar dates in `YYYY-MM-DD` form, with no default, and the range includes both ends. `eventCountPerUser` is computed by this API — the event count divided by the event’s active users — and falls back to the event count when the event has no active users. For traffic per page instead of per event use `GET /v1/analytics/{projectId}/pages`.

parameters.name: startDate
parameters.description: First calendar day of the range, in `YYYY-MM-DD` form. Required, with no default. Inclusive: traffic recorded for this day is included.

parameters.name: endDate
parameters.description: Last calendar day of the range, in `YYYY-MM-DD` form. Required, with no default. Inclusive. An `endDate` earlier than `startDate` is not rejected; it matches no rows.

parameters.name: projectId
parameters.description: ID of the project whose analytics are read. `GET /v1/project` lists the projects the token can see and returns each one’s `id`.

200.description: One row per event name recorded in the range, most frequent first.

eventName.description: Name of the event as Google Analytics recorded it, for example `page_view`, `session_start` or `purchase`.

eventCount.description: Times this event was recorded in the range.

totalUsers.description: Distinct users who triggered the event at least once in the range.

activeUsers.description: Distinct users Google Analytics counted as active: a user is active once they have an engaged session.

totalRevenue.description: Revenue attributed to this event, in the currency of each property. The currency code is not returned.

eventCountPerUser.description: Average number of times a user triggered the event: the event count divided by its active users. When the event has no active users, the event count itself is returned.

data.description: One row per event name recorded in the range, most frequent first.

get.summary: List pages with their traffic metrics
get.description:
A paged table of the pages that had traffic, one row per page, from the Google Analytics 4 properties linked to the project. Rows are keyed by page URL after normalization — host lowercased with a leading `www.` dropped, path and query lowercased, trailing slash trimmed — so the same page reached by differently written URLs collapses into one row.

Both dates are required calendar dates in `YYYY-MM-DD` form, with no default, and the range includes both ends. `page` starts at 1 and `limit` defaults to 20, with anything above 1000 reduced to 1000 rather than rejected. `total` is the number of distinct pages matching `filter`, `pageSize` the number of pages of `limit` rows covering that total, and the sort defaults to `active_users` descending.

Every figure is summed over the stored rows for that one page, which is what separates this table from `GET /v1/analytics/{projectId}`: `userEngagementDuration` is seconds per active user rather than a total, and the two rates are recomputed from the page’s own sessions. A page with no traffic in the range is not in the table.

parameters.name: startDate
parameters.description: First calendar day of the range, in `YYYY-MM-DD` form. Required, with no default. Inclusive: traffic recorded for this day is included.

parameters.name: endDate
parameters.description: Last calendar day of the range, in `YYYY-MM-DD` form. Required, with no default. Inclusive. An `endDate` earlier than `startDate` is not rejected; it matches no rows.

parameters.name: filter
parameters.description: Text that must appear somewhere in the page URL. Matched as a substring; omitted or blank returns every page.

parameters.name: orderBy
parameters.description: Metric to sort by, named as Google Analytics names it and matching one of the row fields: `active_users`, `sessions`, `engaged_sessions`, `screen_page_views` (total views), `engagement_rate`, `bounce_rate`, `user_engagement_duration` (seconds per active user), `event_count`, `conversions`, `total_revenue` or `screen_page_views_per_user` (views per active user). Defaults to `active_users`.

parameters.name: orderDir
parameters.description: Direction of the sort: `asc` for smallest first, `desc` for largest first. `desc` when omitted, which is what a traffic table usually wants.

parameters.name: page
parameters.description: 1-based page number to return. Defaults to 1; a value below 1 or a fraction is rejected.

parameters.name: limit
parameters.description: Rows per page, 1 or more. Defaults to 20 and is capped at 1000: a larger value is reduced to 1000 rather than rejected.

parameters.name: projectId
parameters.description: ID of the project whose analytics are read. `GET /v1/project` lists the projects the token can see and returns each one’s `id`.

200.description: One page of rows, one row per page that had traffic in the range.

total.description: Distinct pages in the range that matched the filter — how many rows the table holds without paging.

limit.description: Rows per page actually applied: the requested `limit` capped at 1000, or 20 when the request sent none.

pageSize.description: Number of pages of `limit` rows needed to cover `total` — a count of pages, not of rows.

pageLocation.description: URL of the page as Google Analytics recorded it, with scheme, host, path and query. Rows group URLs that normalize alike, so this is one of the spellings that merged into the row.

activeUsers.description: Distinct users Google Analytics counted as active: a user is active once they have an engaged session.

sessions.description: Sessions Google Analytics counted. A visit is one session however many pages it covers.

engagedSessions.description: Sessions Google Analytics classes as engaged: those lasting longer than 10 seconds, containing a conversion, or viewing two or more pages.

userEngagementDuration.description: Seconds of engagement time attributed to the page, divided by its active users: time per user, not the total across all users.

eventCount.description: Events recorded, under every event name.

conversions.description: Conversion events — events the property marks as conversions, key events in newer Google Analytics wording.

totalRevenue.description: Revenue from purchases, subscriptions and advertising, in the currency of each property. The currency code is not returned.

engagementRate.description: Engaged sessions divided by sessions, between 0 and 1, and 0 when there are no sessions. Computed by this API from the summed sessions rather than read from Google Analytics.

bounceRate.description: Sessions that were not engaged, divided by all sessions, between 0 and 1 — the exact complement of `engagementRate`, and computed by this API for the same reason.

screenPageViewsPerUser.description: Page views divided by active users. When there are no active users, the page view count itself is returned in place of the ratio.

items.description: The rows for this page, in the requested order.
